name: Statue of John Hope, 4th Earl of Hopetoun
address: Forecourt of Dundas House, 36 St Andrew Square, Edinburgh EH2 2YB
description: A bronze general stands guard over Dundas House's forecourt, toga draped over one shoulder, a horse bowing its head beside him. This is John Hope, 4th Earl of Hopetoun (1765-1823), who took command of the British army at Corunna after Sir John Moore fell in battle. Sculptor Thomas Campbell dressed him as a Roman rather than a soldier, standing rather than mounted - a quieter kind of monument than you might expect for a general. The stepped granite plinth beneath him carries an inscription penned by Sir Walter Scott himself.
interesting_fact_1: It was never meant to be here. Edinburgh commissioned the statue in 1824 for Charlotte Square, then judged it unsuitable; it went unplaced for years until the bank accepted it in 1834 and set it in its own forecourt. The accidental siting produced the square's best in-joke: the Earl stands looking west across the gardens directly at the Melville Monument and Henry Dundas - who was his brother-in-law, having married the Earl's sister Lady Jane Hope in 1793.

name: Lion of Scotland
description: This sleeping lion is carved from 20 tonnes of pink granite, and you're looking at over a year of hand-tool labour with not a single power tool used. Sculptor Ronald Rae carved this from a single boulder of Corrennie granite from Aberdeenshire - some 17 feet nose to tail, 8 feet at the shoulder. It first lay in Holyrood Park, deliberately placed between the Palace of Holyroodhouse and the new Scottish Parliament, beneath Arthur's Seat - a hill long read as a lion in its own right. Now it rests here in St Andrew Square Gardens instead.
interesting_fact_1: It's been voted Edinburgh's best-loved sculpture. When its Holyrood loan was due to expire in 2008, Scottish Blue Badge guides raised a petition and thousands signed it; that won a two-year reprieve, and on 25 April 2010 the lion made the mile-long journey across town.
interesting_fact_2: It came here on loan rather than by purchase, financed by Essential Edinburgh and private sponsors - Rae has said he hopes the city will one day buy it outright. Technically, it is still a visitor.

name: Melville Monument
description: Tip your head back for the full 45 metres of fluted Doric column rising above the gardens, modelled on Trajan's Column in Rome and weighing around 1,500 tons. Robert Stevenson - grandfather of novelist Robert Louis Stevenson, and already Scotland's master lighthouse engineer - helped solve the engineering, since nothing this large had been attempted in the country before. At the top stands Henry Dundas, 1st Viscount Melville, carved by Robert Forrest from a design by Sir Francis Chantrey.
interesting_fact_1: Dundas was so politically powerful in late-18th-century Scotland he was nicknamed 'The Uncrowned King of Scotland' - and this monument is the 'big man in the sky' the game's own clue points players toward. In 1806 he became the last person ever impeached in the UK, for misappropriating public funds.
interesting_fact_2: A plaque added in 2021 addresses his role in delaying the abolition of the slave trade. The £8,000 bill was met by subscription from the officers and men of the Royal Navy, which Dundas had run as First Lord of the Admiralty from 1804.

name: National Portrait Gallery
description: Red sandstone turrets and niche-set statues of famous Scots line this Gothic Revival facade, and you're facing a building whose donor kept his identity secret for seven years. name: James Clerk Maxwell statue
address: Central reservation, east end of George Street at St Andrew Square, Edinburgh EH2 2LL
description: Sit for a moment across from the seated bronze at the top of George Street, and you're facing James Clerk Maxwell (1831-1879), captured mid-thought by sculptor Alexander Stoddart, spinning colour top in hand and his terrier Toby curled at his feet. name: Thistle Court
description: Two plain sandstone houses face each other across this small grass court, and you're standing at the very start of the New Town - the oldest surviving buildings in the whole development, put up in 1767. name: The Dome
description: A hexastyle Corinthian portico towers over George Street - six 35-foot columns, 95 feet wide, topped by a sculpted pediment. name: St Andrew's and St George's West Church
description: Inside, the oval ceiling is lifted straight from an 18th-century engraving of the ruins of Palmyra - the first elliptical church plan built anywhere in Britain. Built in 1784 as St Andrew's Church - the New Town's first - its curved interior was partly a virtue made of necessity, since the leftover plot was too shallow for a conventional nave. name: Susan Ferrier's Home
description: This townhouse is now folded into the InterContinental hotel, and you're looking at the home where novelist Susan Ferrier lived from age two until nearly sixty, writing all three of her novels under this roof. Sometimes called 'the Scottish Jane Austen', she published anonymously - not publicly named as an author until 1851, three years before her death - while her father's position as a Writer to the Signet put her at the heart of Edinburgh's literary establishment, seated beside Walter Scott himself.

name: Hidden Back-Lane White Tiles
description: Duck into this back lane and look up at the white glazed brick lining its walls - a Victorian trick for bouncing daylight into a space the sun never reaches directly. name: The Giant Caryatids
description: The fifth-floor gallery isn't held up by columns at all - four robed female figures carry the weight on their heads instead. name: St Andrew Square
description: This wasn't meant to be Edinburgh's financial quarter - it was supposed to be its grandest address. James Craig's 1767 plan put a church here, mirroring Charlotte Square at the New Town's far end, but banker Sir Lawrence Dundas outbid the city and built Dundas House for himself in 1774. Where one banker led, others followed, and by the century's end this had become Scotland's banking and insurance headquarters - a role the buildings ringing you still play today. For over 200 years the gardens at the centre stayed locked, private to residents and nearby offices only, finally opening to the public for the first time in April 2008.
interesting_fact_1: The 45-metre Melville Monument at the square's centre, modelled on Trajan's Column in Rome, honours Henry Dundas - a politician so dominant over 1790s Scotland that he was nicknamed 'the uncrowned king of Scotland'. He's also this walk's most contested figure: as Home Secretary in 1792 he pushed for a 'gradual' rather than immediate abolition of the slave trade, a delay historians still argue prolonged it by over a decade, and a plaque addressing that history was added to the monument in 2021.
interesting_fact_2: Philosopher David Hume lived just off the square in the 1770s, persuaded to move there by his architect friend Robert Adam, and hosted guests including Benjamin Franklin. Locals nicknamed his street 'Saint David Street' as a joke about the famously atheist philosopher living somewhere named for a saint - and, unusually, the joke stuck: it's still the street's official name today.
interesting_fact_3: Since reopening in 2008 after a £2.6 million refurbishment, these gardens have become one of the city's busiest public spaces, hosting open-air cinema screenings, festival pop-ups and a winter ice rink - a striking reversal for a garden that spent two centuries locked to everyone but the residents overlooking it.

name: George Street
description: Everything about this street was built to impress. George Street sits on the New Town's central ridge, a full storey above Princes Street and Queen Street on either side, so that from up here you can see clear across the Forth to Fife in one direction and the Pentland Hills in the other. James Craig's 1767 grid made it the spine of the whole development, running dead straight between St Andrew Square behind you and Charlotte Square three-quarters of a mile ahead - named for King George III, with the two squares at either end named for his wife and, informally, himself.
interesting_fact_1: George Street was drawn up purely as a residential address, lined with Georgian townhouses for the city's wealthiest families. That changed hard in the Victorian era, when banks and insurance offices - drawn by the street's sheer prestige - bought up the townhouses one by one and rebuilt their fronts as grand banking halls, which is why you'll spot far more columns and pediments here than on any ordinary residential street.
interesting_fact_2: In 1822, George Street hosted the social event of the century: a Peers' Ball at the Assembly Rooms in honour of King George IV's state visit, the first by a reigning monarch to Scotland in almost 170 years. The whole street was said to be gridlocked with carriages that night.

name: Thomas Chalmers Statue
address: George Street at Castle Street, Edinburgh
description: At the Castle Street corner stands a bronze man in Moderator's robes, Bible cradled on one forearm, his other hand marking the page as if mid-sermon. The plinth beneath him is bare red granite, cut only with his name and dates - no list of achievements, because in 1843 he didn't need one. On 18 May that year, Thomas Chalmers led roughly a third of the ministers at the Church of Scotland's General Assembly out of St Andrew's and St George's Church, back along this very street, in protest at the state's grip on who churches could appoint. Crowds cheered them through Edinburgh as they founded the Free Church of Scotland on the spot, with Chalmers as its first Moderator and a fund already drawn up to support the hundreds of ministers who'd just walked away from their salaries. Sir John Steell cast this statue in 1878, three decades later, and put him back exactly where it happened.
interesting_fact_1: Steell, who cast this statue in 1878, was Scotland's leading monumental sculptor of the century - the same hand behind the seated marble Scott inside the Scott Monument and the mounted Duke of Wellington outside Register House on Princes Street.

name: View Down Castle Street to the Castle
address: Castle Street at George Street, Edinburgh
description: From this junction, the view south does exactly what it was drawn to do: Castle Street runs dead straight for a quarter mile before Edinburgh Castle rises above the rooftops on its volcanic crag, framed neatly by tenements on either side. That's not an accident of geography - it's James Craig's New Town plan working precisely as designed over two centuries later. Craig's original 1766 competition entry was far fussier than what got built: a diagonal web of radiating streets around a central square, loosely modelled on the Union flag. Edinburgh's town council thought it impractical and sent him back to the drawing board, and what came out was the plainer grid you're standing in now - a set of parallel streets whose cross-streets, this one included, were deliberately aligned and named so that looking down them would always lead your eye somewhere worth seeing.
interesting_fact_1: Craig's original 1766 prize-winning competition entry was far fussier than what actually got built: a diagonal layout of radiating streets around a central square, loosely inspired by the Union flag. Edinburgh's town council judged it impractical, and Craig reworked it into the plainer grid of parallel streets that exists today - the same plan whose cross-streets, this one included, were given these deliberate, view-aligned names.

name: Walter Scott's House
description: Picture candlelight before dawn behind the plain sash windows on the first floor: this is where Sir Walter Scott wrote, often starting at 5am, hours before his day job at the Court of Session began. He and his family used this handsome three-storey townhouse as their winter home from 1801 to 1826, and it was here - at what he affectionately nicknamed 'the cabin' - that he produced the bulk of the Waverley novels that made him the best-selling author in Europe. The ending wasn't so tidy: in January 1826 his printing and publishing partnerships collapsed under debts of well over £100,000, and rather than declare bankruptcy he spent the rest of his life writing to pay it off, a decision that broke his health. He recorded leaving for the last time in his journal: 'This morning I leave No. 39 Castle Street for the last time... So farewell, poor 39.'
interesting_fact_1: J.M.W. Turner painted this house in 1834, two years after Scott's death, in a work he titled simply 'Former Residence of Walter Scott.'

name: The Oxford Bar
description: Push through the door on Young Street and notice what's missing: no music, no fruit machines, no television, just a corridor of small rooms and the low murmur of regulars over pies and a well-kept range of beer and whisky. The pub has traded here since at least 1811, though deeds show it was still a confectioner's shop as late as 1843, only becoming a bar for good once formally handed to wine merchant Andrew Wilson in 1893. It stayed a quiet local secret until Ian Rankin, drawn partly because it was a genuine off-duty haunt for Edinburgh police officers, made it the fictional local of Inspector Rebus from the character's 1987 debut. True to form, the Oxford Bar has stayed famously indifferent to its own fame - no Rebus merchandise, no themed decor, just the same compartmentalised layout it's kept since being Category B listed in 1966.
interesting_fact_1: Willie Ross, the first-ever official occupant of Bute House up on Charlotte Square at the far end of this walk, was also known to drink here.

name: Church of Scotland Offices
description: This one doesn't match its neighbours: a steep double-pitched mansard roof and heavy dark stonework that reads closer to Stockholm than to the pale Georgian terraces on either side. Nicknamed 'one-two-one' inside Church circles for its street number, it was built in 1909-11 to a design by Edinburgh architect Sydney Mitchell for the United Free Church of Scotland - descended from the Free Church that Thomas Chalmers founded after leading a third of ministers out of the General Assembly in 1843, whose statue stands a short walk back along this street. Only when the two churches reunited in 1929, healing that 86-year rift, did this building's name finally become accurate. A matching bookshop extension went up next door at 119 George Street in the 1930s, and it remains the Church of Scotland's administrative headquarters today.
interesting_fact_1: A planned matching extension on the west side of the building was never built, though the church went on to buy the neighbouring property regardless; the bookshop wing that did get built sits on the opposite side, at 119 George Street.

name: Kimpton Charlotte Square Hotel
address: 38 Charlotte Square, Edinburgh (corner of George Street)
description: At the corner where George Street opens out into Charlotte Square, a pilastered stone facade - it's part of Robert Adam's 1791 unified 'palace front' scheme for the square, continued after his death in 1792 by his successor as the Crown's Scottish architect, Robert Reid, who reworked the design in 1810. Two of these grand townhouses, numbers 38 and 39, were knocked together into a hotel in the 1870s, with more of the terrace absorbed over later decades. It traded for generations as the Roxburghe Hotel before a 2019 rebrand turned it into the Kimpton Charlotte Square - new name, new interiors, but the same Adam-Reid facade above street level that householders here would still recognise, looking out now at the domed former church across the gardens that Reid built on the site Adam never got to finish.
interesting_fact_1: Architects kept adapting the shell of Adam's 1791 townhouses rather than replacing them as the building passed from private residence to hotel through several names and refits - guests today sleep behind the same pilastered facade Adam drew for householders who never imagined a hotel there.

name: Prince Albert Memorial
description: Even from behind the railings - because these gardens stay locked to everyone except keyholders most of the year - the scale of this thing is obvious: a 30-foot bronze of Prince Albert in Field Marshal's uniform, rearing on his horse above a granite pedestal at the centre of the square. Queen Victoria commissioned it after Albert's sudden death from typhoid in December 1861, but it took Sir John Steell fifteen years to finish and unveil it, by which point several other Albert memorials already stood elsewhere in Britain. Victoria came in person on 17 August 1876 to unveil her husband's statue and knighted Steell on the spot. The horse itself was cast from a single piece with no visible joins, reckoned a technical feat at the time.
interesting_fact_1: The four bronze figure groups ringing the base were each cast by a different sculptor - William Brodie's Nobility, Clark Stanton's Army and Navy, and David Watson Stevenson's Labour and Science and Learning - while the stone plinth beneath them was designed by architect David Bryce, better known for his baronial mansions and the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh.

name: West Register House
description: A green copper dome and gilt cupola rise some 160 feet above the square, and it's worth knowing what used to happen underneath it: hymn-singing. Built in 1811-14 as St George's Church to designs by Robert Reid - who reworked an earlier scheme Robert Adam had drawn for the same site before his death in 1792 - it opened in 1814 with room for around 1,600 worshippers beneath a dome deliberately styled to echo St Paul's Cathedral in London. St George's closed as a congregation in 1964, merging with St Andrew's Church further along George Street, where Thomas Chalmers led his 1843 walkout. By 1970 the sacred interior had been gutted and refitted with five storeys of fireproof archive stacks, reopening as West Register House - now holding some of the nation's oldest legal documents under the dome once built for worship.
interesting_fact_1: The building's own structure eventually threatened it: the wood-and-stone construction beneath the dome developed severe defects that forced the closure of the church and drove the decision to gut the interior and rebuild it as fireproof archive stacks in the 1960s.

name: The Georgian House
description: No.7's front door is the threshold of a house frozen at the height of Georgian fashion - the National Trust for Scotland runs it now as a museum, furnished exactly as it would have looked when new. It was built in 1796 for John Lamont, 18th Chief of Clan Lamont, who lived here with his family until 1815; he bought it for a little over £1,800 and sold it twenty years later for £3,000, trying and failing to offset debts that were sinking his clan's finances. From 1889 it was home to theologian Rev Alexander Whyte and his wife Jane, who raised eight children within these walls, and the Marquess of Bute bought the house in 1927. On the 5th Marquess's death in 1956, it passed to the National Trust in part settlement of death duties, restored and opened to the public in 1975 - standing directly next door to No.6, Bute House, official residence of Scotland's First Minister since 1999.
interesting_fact_1: For decades before it became a museum, No.7 served as an antique dealer's showroom - the very trade the house now exists to interpret, minus the historical accuracy.

name: Bute House
description: The elegant pilastered door of No.6 is the working home of Scotland's First Minister, though the story starts long before devolution. Robert Adam designed it in 1791 as part of his grand vision for the whole square, though he died the following year, before it was finished. The plot was first sold in 1792 to Orlando Hart, an Edinburgh shoemaker and town councillor, for a modest £290. The house later spent decades as a hotel - in 1832 the exiled King Charles X of France stayed here briefly while it traded as Oman's Hotel, and some of the hotel's original brass lettering is still visible on the building today. The Marquess of Bute bought it in 1922 and spent decades restoring Adam's design before it was preserved for the nation and renamed Bute House in 1966, with William Ross, Secretary of State for Scotland, installed as its first official resident.
interesting_fact_1: William Ross, installed as the first official resident when the house was renamed Bute House in 1966, was known to be a regular down at the Oxford Bar on Young Street, a few minutes' walk from this door.

name: The Alexander Graham Bell
description: Above one of the doorways here is something older than the pub itself: a carved lintel reading 'God bless the baxters of Edinburgh who built this house 1675', a nod to the city's medieval baker's guild and a much earlier building that once stood on this corner. The Georgian townhouses in front of you actually date from around 1785, and traded for years as the Ivory Lounge before JD Wetherspoon took the site over in May 2010 and renamed it after the inventor said to have been born just around the corner. Alexander Graham Bell really was born nearby, at 16 South Charlotte Street. He patented the telephone in 1876 while teaching in Boston, emigrated permanently to North America as a young man, and kept his ties to his home city throughout his life.
interesting_fact_1: Bell was made a Freeman of Edinburgh in 1920, more than four decades after the invention that made him famous, and kept returning to visit his home city throughout his life.

name: The Cambridge Bar
description: Young Street is one of the New Town's quiet service lanes, tucked just behind George Street's grander frontages, sharing this short stretch with an even more famous neighbour a few doors along: the spartan, traditional Oxford Bar, world-famous as the fictional haunt of Ian Rankin's Inspector Rebus. This two-storey Georgian corner bar takes the opposite approach - a craft beer and gourmet burger menu served downstairs in an L-shaped room full of wooden alcoves, low tables and leather benches, with an upstairs room for private functions and overflow dining. The two pubs, one named for Oxford and one for Cambridge, sit on the same lane purely by coincidence rather than design, making for a natural point of comparison between the Oxford's famously spartan interior and the Cambridge's more contemporary take.
interesting_fact_1: Young Street was originally the westernmost stretch of Thistle Street before being split off and renamed after John Young, the developer paid £20 to buy the very first plot sold in Edinburgh's New Town in 1767 - an incentive that helped kick-start the whole development. Young's own Thistle Court, built that same year, still stands nearby as the oldest surviving building in the New Town.

name: Browns Restaurant
description: Take a seat at one of Browns' pavement tables and you're dining behind a distinguished architectural facade. These category B-listed townhouses at 131-133 George Street went up between 1780 and 1790 as part of the New Town's original terrace, altered by architect John Bryce in 1883. William Burn, one of the era's most sought-after architects, kept his office at No.131 from 1822; after 1844 his former assistant and eventual partner David Bryce - designer of Fettes College and the Royal Infirmary - worked from the same address. No.133 next door had its own notable residents: the great portraitist Sir Henry Raeburn lived there for a time, followed later by novelist Catherine Sinclair. The building later passed through spells as the Leicester Permanent Building Society's offices and, more recently, a hairdressers, before becoming part of Browns' brasserie.
interesting_fact_1: Raeburn's own likenesses of Sir Walter Scott and the skating Reverend Robert Walker rank among Scotland's best-known images, and his studio on nearby York Place still stands - an easy walk from this same George Street frontage he'd have crossed daily.

name: Charlotte Square
description: James Craig's original 1767 plan named this square after King George III and gave it the same footprint as St Andrew Square at the New Town's other end - a matching bookend, symmetrical right down to the name. It was renamed Charlotte Square in 1786, for the King's queen, to stop confusion with a different George Square over in the Old Town. Robert Adam won the commission for its unifying design in 1791, his last major work before his death the following year - one long palace-like frontage on the north side, disguising what's actually a row of separate townhouses behind it, an idea barely tried in Scotland before this.
interesting_fact_1: Adam's north side is the one everyone photographs, but he didn't design the whole square - after his death in 1792, other architects filled in the remaining three sides more plainly, which is why the square looks subtly less grand the further you get from that one iconic Adam frontage.
interesting_fact_2: From 1983 to 2020, these private gardens became a different kind of stage every August: the Edinburgh International Book Festival pitched its tents on this lawn for 38 years running, turning Adam's genteel square into one of the world's biggest literary gatherings before the festival moved elsewhere in 2021.

address: Rose Street at South Charlotte Street, Edinburgh
description: This thousand-metre run of pubs, bars and restaurants, and you're standing at the start of what Victorian Edinburgh called faintly disreputable after dark - the street its own pub crawl nicknamed the 'Amber Mile'. Laid out by James Craig in 1767 as a modest service lane behind George Street's grand townhouses, it's this trade character, not the architecture, that made Rose Street famous. The crawl traditionally starts right here on your left at Scott's, 202 Rose Street - dating to 1790, named for a formidable 19th-century landlady, 'Ma Scott', still advertised on the pub's own sign today.
interesting_fact_1: Pedestrianised by the 1970s, Rose Street runs some 1,000 metres in total to St Andrew Square; this walk follows only its westernmost stretch.

name: Charlotte Chapel / Rose Theatre
description: This plain, dignified stone hall, and you'd never guess it once held a Baptist congregation of 1,000 - or that it's now a four-stage theatre. Built in 1912 to a design by J A Arnott and J Inch Morrison, this was Charlotte Chapel, founded in January 1808 by evangelist Christopher Anderson, who began preaching in the Pleasance before outgrowing that hall and relocating here. Its restrained exterior gives little away about the busy life that has filled it for over two centuries.

Danish choreographer Peter Schaufuss bought the deconsecrated chapel that year for £1.8 million and reopened it in 2017 as the Rose Theatre, now a year-round performing arts venue and Fringe hub.
interesting_fact_2: As of 2026, a hotel conversion with a rooftop bar has already been approved for the building - so the theatre you're looking at may prove just one more phase in a longer story.

Artist Astrid Jaekel designed the piece first as intricate hand-cut paper before Pentland Precision Engineering translated it into weatherproof steel, commissioned around 2012-13 by Essential Edinburgh as a nod to the 'Rose Street Poets' who once drank in its pubs.

Jaekel chose it after realising the building's seven arched windows matched its seven verses exactly.
interesting_fact_2: The work was shortlisted for the 2013 Adrian Henri Prize for Poetry in Art and the 2014 Association of Illustrators Awards.

description: The paving beneath your feet on this block, and you're standing on a small piece of Edinburgh planning history - in 1973 it became the first street in the city closed to traffic and paved for pedestrians only, years ahead of Rose Street's other blocks or even Princes Street. In the 1980s, artist Maggy Howarth set eight large circular pebble mosaics into the surface at its side-street junctions, each a different rose design worked entirely from small stones, sturdy enough to carry delivery vans.

name: McVitie's Original Shop
description: This unremarkable shopfront marks where one of Britain's best-known biscuit makers began. In 1830, Robert McVitie ran a modest provision shop from here, baking and selling bread and confectionery to Rose Street's working trade decades before the family name became a household word - one workshop among many that gave the street its tradesman's character in the shadow of George Street's banks.

Grant's recipe is still the one used today, guarded as a trade secret for well over a century.

name: The Kenilworth
description: Behind this unassuming Rose Street frontage are blue-and-white Minton tiles running floor-to-ceiling under brown-and-white banding, beneath a patterned red-and-cream plasterwork ceiling. The building dates to around 1780, but the ornate interior you're standing in is the work of architect Thomas Purves Marwick, fitted out in 1899 and trading as the Kenilworth by 1904, named for Sir Walter Scott's 1821 novel. It's Category A listed - Rose Street's highest heritage grade.
interesting_fact_1: Scott supplies the theme at one remove: further along Rose Street stands the Abbotsford, named after the house Scott built himself - two pubs, one novelist, one street.

name: Alexander Graham Bell Birthplace
description: A green door with a small carved plaque beside it marks the flat where Alexander Graham Bell was born on 3 March 1847. His father, Alexander Melville Bell, was a renowned elocutionist who ran a school from here training teachers of the deaf using his own 'Visible Speech' system - work the young Bell grew up around, and would later echo in Boston. Both his mother and, eventually, his wife were deaf, a thread that ran through his life long before the invention that made him famous.
interesting_fact_1: The plaque beside the door still reads simply: 'Alexander Graham Bell, Inventor of the Telephone, Born here 3rd March 1847.'

name: St John's Episcopal Church
address: St John's Church, Princes Street, Edinburgh EH2 4BJ
description: Inside, the plaster fan-vaulted ceiling, modelled on the Henry VII Chapel at Westminster Abbey - the single most striking feature of this Gothic Revival church marking the western gateway into Princes Street Gardens. Architect William Burn was only 25 when he designed it; building began in 1816 and it was dedicated as St John's Chapel on Maundy Thursday 1818. An Act of Parliament passed the same year banned any further building on the north side of Princes Street, specifically to protect views of the Castle.
interesting_fact_1: In 2002 a tabot - a sacred replica of the Tablets of the Law used in Ethiopian Orthodox worship - turned up among the church's possessions and was quietly returned to Addis Ababa.

name: St Cuthbert's Parish Church
description: This churchyard, tucked just below St John's, sits on ground worshipped continuously for longer than almost anywhere else in Edinburgh. Tradition holds that St Cuthbert founded a church here around AD 670, and the site is first documented in a charter of about 1127. The current building, opened in 1894 to a design by Hippolyte Blanc, is only the latest in a long line on this spot - when the previous Georgian church of 1775 was demolished, evidence of six earlier buildings beneath it was reportedly found.
interesting_fact_1: Buried here: essayist Thomas De Quincey, logarithms inventor John Napier, and William Macao, reckoned the first naturalised Chinese citizen in Scotland.

name: Ross Fountain
address: West Princes Street Gardens, Edinburgh EH1 2EU
description: Nude and semi-nude figures rise in three tiers above you - an unlikely sight beneath Edinburgh Castle's ramparts. Cast in ornate French Second Empire style at the Durenne foundry in France and shown at the 1862 International Exhibition in London, Edinburgh gunmaker Daniel Ross bought it for £2,000 and gave it to the city. Shipped north to Leith in 122 separate pieces, it was bolted back together and installed here in 1872.
interesting_fact_1: Victorian Edinburgh was reportedly uneasy about the figures' undress when it first went up in 1872; some nineteenth-century guidebooks tiptoed around describing them too closely.

name: Norwegian Memorial Stone
address: West Princes Street Gardens (terrace path near Castle Street), Edinburgh EH2 3AA
description: A weathered grey boulder of Norwegian gneiss sits beside the path, propped on three smaller stones of the same rock, a single inscription carved into it. It was presented to Edinburgh on 18 September 1978 by veterans of the Norwegian Brigade, the exiled force raised and trained in Scotland during the Second World War after Norway fell to German occupation in 1940. General Sir Roland Gibbs accepted it on behalf of the British Army, asking the Lord Provost to take the stone into the city's care.
interesting_fact_1: It sits within sight of a bear who served in a different exiled army raised in Scotland during the very same war: Wojtek, of the Polish 2nd Corps, memorialised a few dozen metres away.

name: Scottish American War Memorial
address: West Princes Street Gardens (near Castle Street), Edinburgh EH2 3AP
description: A bronze kilted infantryman kneels before you, gazing toward Castle Rock, backed by a frieze of soldiers marching off behind a piper. Titled 'The Call 1914', it was sculpted by Robert Tait McKenzie, a Scottish-Canadian based at the University of Pennsylvania, and took him around four years to complete; the figures were cast at the Roman Bronze Works in Brooklyn before shipping to Scotland. It was unveiled on 7 September 1927 by the American Ambassador, Alanson B. Houghton.
interesting_fact_1: The frieze behind the soldier shows ordinary civilians falling into step behind a piper as they turn into recruits - a visual telling of exactly what the title describes. It stands close enough to Wojtek's own memorial that both can be seen from the same stretch of path.

name: Wojtek the Soldier Bear Memorial
address: West Princes Street Gardens, Edinburgh (near Castle Street terrace path)
description: A bronze soldier walks beside a bear at one-and-a-quarter life size, one hand resting on its back - this is Wojtek - a Syrian brown bear cub bought from a boy in Iran in 1942 by Polish soldiers on their way to war. He grew up inside the 22nd Artillery Supply Company, drinking beer, wrestling the men and eating cigarettes. Unveiled on 7 November 2015, the memorial is the work of Scottish sculptor Alan Beattie Herriot, cast at Powderhall Bronze here in Edinburgh, with a bronze relief panel behind tracing his wartime journey.
interesting_fact_1: The granite the pair stand on was quarried at Strzegom in Poland and shipped to Edinburgh, so that the soldier and his bear would always have a piece of their homeland underfoot.

Diageo, the drinks giant behind Johnnie Walker, poured £185 million into the project, the single largest investment ever made in Scotch whisky tourism, transforming the old Binns store into tasting rooms, interactive galleries and a rooftop bar looking straight across the city to Edinburgh Castle.

name: Police Box Cafe
description: This pastel pink-and-green kiosk is one of Edinburgh's old police boxes - miniature one-person police stations that once stood on street corners across the city, now doing a brisk trade in coffee instead of crime-fighting. City architect Ebenezer MacRae designed the model from 1933, giving each box a pediment, pilasters and cast-iron panelling deliberately styled to blend into the New Town's neo-classical streetscape rather than stand out as municipal furniture.
interesting_fact_1: Despite the resemblance, these are not the same design as Doctor Who's TARDIS - that's modelled on London's police box, a different pattern entirely. Sources vary on the original total (widely cited figures range from around 85 up to 142 boxes built across the city from 1933).
interesting_fact_2: In 2014 the police sold off another 14 of their remaining boxes, keeping just one for themselves. Most survivors, like this one, have been repurposed as coffee kiosks, flower stalls or takeaway hatches - a genuine recurring sight worth spotting elsewhere on this walk.

name: The Caledonian Hotel
description: Red sandstone rises above Princes Street here, quarried at Locharbriggs and Corncockle in Dumfriesshire and brought in on the Caledonian Railway Company's own trains. Built between 1899 and 1903 as the grand terminus hotel for Princes Street Station, arriving passengers could once step straight from the platforms through three archways into the hotel itself. Long known simply as 'The Caley', it outlived the station by decades: passenger trains stopped running in September 1965, but the hotel above kept operating.
interesting_fact_1: The Caledonian's engineers once piped waste steam from locomotives at the adjoining station straight into the hotel's boilers to help heat its water - a literal recycling of the railway's own exhaust. Its corridors are noticeably wide, reputedly built generously enough for two Edwardian ladies in full hooped skirts to pass without their dresses touching.
interesting_fact_2: Over the twentieth century its guest book filled with the famous - Charlie Chaplin, Laurel and Hardy, Elizabeth Taylor, Gene Kelly, who is said to have danced down the main staircase, and Sean Connery, a regular guest until his death in 2020. More recently Taylor Swift stayed here during her 2024 Eras Tour dates in Edinburgh.

name: Dean Ramsay Memorial
address: St John's Episcopal Church, Princes Street, Edinburgh EH1 2EP
description: This soaring Celtic cross, over 8 metres of Shap granite on three broad steps, stands in the graveyard of St John's Episcopal Church. It commemorates Edward Bannerman Ramsay, the church's minister for over 40 years and Dean of Edinburgh from 1841 until his death in 1872. Designed by architect Robert Rowand Anderson and erected in 1879, the cross carries bronze relief panels cast by F. A. Skidmore of Coventry, depicting scenes from Christ's Passion alongside six acts of charity - fitting for a man remembered as much for his philanthropy as his ministry.
interesting_fact_1: Ramsay was also a co-founder of Glenalmond College, one of Scotland's leading independent schools.

name: Mather's Bar
description: This single-room corner bar has an interior that's changed remarkably little in well over a century - high ceilings with ornate plasterwork, a large stained-glass window, floor-to-ceiling tiling in the porch, and an original bar counter and half-height panelling. Wine merchant Hugh Mather took over the ground floor of this 1900 building in 1902 and established the licensed premises the following year, giving the pub its name, still running in gold lettering across the frontage: 'Wines. H.P. Mather. Spirits.'
interesting_fact_1: CAMRA has identified Mather's as having a nationally important historic pub interior, one of a small number in Scotland to earn that distinction - meaning the fixtures and layout are protected as being of outstanding historic value, not just an old-looking pub but a genuinely preserved one.

name: Statue of Sir James Young Simpson
description: This seated bronze figure in academic robes, book resting on one knee, erected by public subscription in 1877 and designed by sculptor William Brodie. It commemorates Sir James Young Simpson, professor of midwifery at Edinburgh University, who in November 1847 became the first doctor to demonstrate chloroform's use as an anaesthetic - testing it first on himself and two colleagues at his own dinner table before adopting it in his obstetric practice. The discovery transformed surgery and childbirth almost overnight.
interesting_fact_1: Chloroform anaesthesia faced fierce religious objection at first - some clergy argued that easing the pain of childbirth defied the biblical curse on Eve - until Queen Victoria herself was given chloroform during the birth of Prince Leopold in 1853, an endorsement that effectively ended the controversy overnight.
interesting_fact_2: Simpson was knighted in 1866, the first doctor in Scotland to receive the honour, and when he died in 1870 more than 100,000 people are said to have lined Edinburgh's streets for his funeral procession to Warriston Cemetery.

name: Princes Street
description: Here's the oddity: Edinburgh's most famous street has buildings running down only one side of it. James Craig's 1767 plan left the north side of Princes Street open on purpose, so residents - and later, everyone - would keep an unbroken view south across the valley to the Old Town and the Castle on its crag. That valley used to be underwater, the old Nor Loch, drained as the New Town went up, and its bed became Princes Street Gardens - still open ground today for exactly the reason Craig intended.
interesting_fact_1: Princes Street wasn't named for any prince in particular - it honours King George III's sons in general, the same way George Street and Princes Street Gardens do. The King himself reportedly disliked the street's originally planned name, 'St Giles Street', because it reminded him of a notorious London slum, and had it changed.
interesting_fact_2: By the 1880s, Edinburgh Council had taken the gardens over from the residents who'd previously kept them private, and the street itself was already shifting from grand townhouses to shops - the start of its long run as Scotland's busiest retail street, a role it still holds today even as almost all the townhouses behind those shopfronts have vanished.

name: Ross Bandstand
description: Edinburgh Castle rises directly above this natural bowl of West Princes Street Gardens, its ramparts framing whatever's happening on the curved stage in front of you. That stage - officially the Ross Open Air Theatre - has stood here since 1935, built to a design by city architect E. J. Macrae after storms wrecked the original 1877 bandstand, a gift from whisky baron William Henry Ross. Around 2,500 people can pack these grassy slopes for the Edinburgh International Festival, the Jazz Festival, Hogmanay concerts and the Festival fireworks that light up the castle overhead. Behind that seemingly settled scene sits nearly two decades of quiet warfare over what should stand here instead.
interesting_fact_1: In 2018, blackout boards erected around summer concerts here blocked the classic view of Edinburgh Castle from Princes Street. The barriers triggered an online backlash strong enough that the council leader ordered them torn down.

name: Royal Scots Greys Monument
address: Princes Street, opposite Frederick Street, Edinburgh
description: A bronze cavalryman stares back across the valley toward Edinburgh Castle, his horse rearing on a rough-hewn rock pedestal above the gardens. Sculptor William Birnie Rhind, working with Alessandro Parlanti, cast him between 1903 and 1906 to commemorate the Royal Scots Greys' dead from the Second Boer War, and Lord Rosebery unveiled the finished monument in 1906. The rider wears the exact uniform the regiment carried to South Africa in 1899, bearskin cap included. By then the Greys were already more than two centuries old, one of the British Army's oldest cavalry regiments, raised back in 1678.
interesting_fact_1: Both the man and the horse are portraits, not composites. The rider was modelled on real Sergeant-Major Anthony James Hinnigan, and the horse beneath him is Polly, who genuinely served with the regiment in South Africa and was cast from life. Plaques added after both World Wars later extended the memorial to the regiment's dead from those conflicts too, so a monument raised for one war ended up carrying the names of three.

name: The Mound
description: Feel the ground level out beneath your feet: this sloped crossing between West and East Princes Street Gardens isn't natural land at all, it's spoil. Between the 1780s and about 1830, an estimated 1.5 million cartloads of earth and rubble dug from the New Town's foundations were tipped here into the drained bed of the old Nor Loch, gradually building a shortcut between the medieval Old Town above and the new Georgian streets across the valley. Macadamised and landscaped by 1830, it now carries the Royal Scottish Academy and the Scottish National Gallery on its slopes - an entire hillside built from someone else's foundations.
interesting_fact_1: Locals called the original crossing 'Geordie Boyd's Brig', after an Old Town clothier named George Boyd who, around 1780, started laying wooden planks across a tip of rubble simply so he could walk over and see the new streets being built. The town council only turned his shortcut into an official project two years later, decreeing in 1782 that all New Town excavation spoil be dumped there systematically. And in 1959, engineers laid an experimental 'electric blanket' heating system beneath the road surface to melt winter ice - long disused, but still down there under everyone's feet.

name: Allan Ramsay Monument
address: West Princes Street Gardens, foot of the Mound, Edinburgh
description: The soft cap on this marble head is a joke about the man's first career. Sir John Steell carved this ten-foot Carrara marble figure of poet and bookseller Allan Ramsay (1686-1758) in 1865, showing him with a book in one hand and a pencil in the other, on a pedestal designed by architect David Bryce. Before Ramsay became a founding figure of the early Edinburgh Enlightenment - opening one of Britain's first circulating libraries and writing the pastoral comedy 'The Gentle Shepherd' - he trained and worked as a wigmaker, and Steell dressed him in his own nightcap rather than the powdered wig he'd once have sold customers. Medallion portraits of his descendants, including painter son Allan Ramsay the Younger, decorate the pedestal sides.
interesting_fact_1: Look down: the mechanism driving the Floral Clock just along the path isn't housed in its own box at all, it's built into the base of this very pedestal. The original 1903 clockwork, made by James Ritchie & Son, was even assembled partly from parts salvaged out of a dismantled church clock in Elie, Fife.

name: Gardener's Cottage
address: Princes Street Gardens (foot of the Mound), Edinburgh EH2 2HG
description: Green barge-boarding under broad eaves marks a Head Gardener's house, not a folly - built in 1886 to a design by city architect Robert Morham from squared, snecked red sandstone. It sits right where the Gardens' two halves meet at the foot of the Mound, so close to the dividing line that even official sources can't agree whether to file it under West or East Princes Street Gardens. No one has lived here for years: the interior was refurbished with period furniture and antiques in 2017, and the cottage now serves as campaign base for the Quaich Project, a City of Edinburgh Council and Ross Development Trust partnership working to reimagine the gardens around it.
interesting_fact_1: The project based here takes its name, and its concept, from the quaich - the traditional Highland 'sharing cup' - because the bowl-shaped hollow of West Princes Street Gardens itself echoes the shape of one, and the project wants the space to bring people together the same way a shared cup does.

name: Floral Clock
address: West Princes Street Gardens, foot of the Mound, Edinburgh
description: Watch the minute hand and you're watching thousands of individual bedding plants, not gears, since the moving parts here are entirely underground. Switched on 10 June 1903, this was the earliest floral clock in Britain and among the first anywhere in the world: city parks superintendent John McHattie designed the planting scheme with advice from James Mossman, a descendant of Mary Queen of Scots' court jeweller, while Edinburgh clockmakers James Ritchie & Son built the hidden mechanism. It started with only an hour hand; a minute hand followed in 1904, and a mechanical cuckoo has called the quarter-hours from a little house beside the clock since 1953.
interesting_fact_1: The clock's mechanism isn't housed on its own at all - it's built into the plinth of the neighbouring Allan Ramsay Monument. The original 1903 clockwork even reused parts salvaged from a dismantled church clock in Elie, Fife, before the whole system was finally converted to electric drive in 1973.

name: Royal Scottish Academy Building
description: The figure crowning the pediment isn't a symbol of wisdom, whatever guidebooks might suggest at a glance - it's Queen Victoria, sculpted as Britannia. William Henry Playfair designed this Greek Doric temple front in 1822-26 as the Royal Institution, home in turn to the Royal Society of Edinburgh and the Board of Manufactures before the Royal Scottish Academy took permanent occupancy in 1911. Before Playfair could build on this spot at all, roughly 2,000 timber piles had to be driven into the soft ground of the old drained Nor Loch bed beneath your feet. Sir John Steell added that rooftop sculpture and the corner sphinxes; the building still hosts rotating exhibitions today, including the RSA's own annual show.
interesting_fact_1: Playfair's original plan for the pediment put the Greek goddess of wisdom, Pallas Athena, up there instead. The design changed, and in 1844 Steell's Victoria-as-Britannia went up in her place - not long after the young queen had come to the throne.

name: John Wilson Statue
description: This bronze figure holds a half-open manuscript and a quill, caught mid-thought - and the pose suits a man who lived two lives at once. Sir John Steell sculpted Professor John Wilson (1785-1854) and unveiled him on 25 March 1865, the same day as the nearby Allan Ramsay statue. Wilson held the Chair of Moral Philosophy at Edinburgh University from 1820 to 1851, teaching by day, while by night - under the pen-name 'Christopher North' - he was the swaggering, pseudonymous voice of the Tory literary journal Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, writing more than fifty articles for it in 1834 alone.
interesting_fact_1: As Christopher North, Wilson co-created 'Noctes Ambrosianae', a long-running series of fictional tavern conversations mixing literary criticism with drinking talk - featuring a character based on his real-life friend, the poet James Hogg.

name: Scottish National Gallery
description: From the lawn, the neoclassical front was, in Prince Albert's own words at the 1850 foundation-stone ceremony, 'a temple erected to the Fine Arts.' William Henry Playfair designed this home for Scotland's national collection of Old Master and Scottish paintings, and it opened to the public in 1859. It stands immediately south of Playfair's earlier Royal Scottish Academy building on the same ridge, the two structures forming a matched pair astride the Mound - though what you're looking at is actually a scaled-down version of his original, more ambitious design, rejected at the time as too expensive.
interesting_fact_1: Even the cheaper version came with an eccentric extra no one built: plans made public in 2025 for the gallery's 175th anniversary revealed that Victorian engineers had drawn up proposals for a swimming bath in the basement. It never happened, but the Weston Link, opened underground in 2019 as part of the £32 million Playfair Project, now connects the gallery directly to the Royal Scottish Academy next door and down into the gardens below.

name: Playfair Steps
description: This broad flight of stone steps is one of the busiest staircases in the city, dropping from Market Street down to the wide paved forecourt between the Royal Scottish Academy and the Scottish National Gallery. Built around 1828 and named after architect William Henry Playfair, they form one of the main pedestrian links between the Old Town above and Princes Street Gardens below. During the Edinburgh Festival Fringe every August, the steps and the plaza at their foot turn into one of the city's busiest informal stages, packed all summer with street performers, jugglers and the crowds who stop to watch them.
interesting_fact_1: The steps closed for four years during construction work on the adjoining National Galleries site and only reopened to the public in July 2023 - a long wait for what is, in normal times, one of the most heavily used staircases in Edinburgh.

name: Adam Black Statue
description: This bronze figure wears the robes of Lord Provost, and the scroll in his hand hints at a career built on paper rather than politics. Sculptor John Hutchison cast Adam Black (1784-1874) in 1877, three years after his death. Black started out as a humble bookseller's apprentice before founding the publishing house A & C Black, bringing out the 7th, 8th and 9th editions of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, serving two terms as Lord Provost of Edinburgh, and sitting as one of the city's MPs from 1856 to 1865.
interesting_fact_1: Black's biggest single gamble paid off spectacularly: in 1851 his firm paid £27,000, an enormous sum at the time, to buy the copyright and printing stock of Sir Walter Scott's Waverley novels, then republished them in cheap shilling editions that put Scott's fiction into ordinary readers' hands for the first time - and turned a solid profit for A & C Black in the process.

name: David Livingstone Statue
address: East Princes Street Gardens, next to the Scott Monument, Edinburgh
description: This bronze figure strides forward mid-step, cloak swinging, a Bible in one hand and a lion skin draped at his side. Sculptor Amelia Robertson Hill cast explorer and missionary David Livingstone (1813-1873), and it was unveiled here on 15 August 1876, just three years after his death in what is now Zambia. That lion skin isn't decorative - it recalls an 1844 mauling in which a lion crushed his arm and shoulder, an injury that left him unable to raise that arm fully overhead for the rest of his life, even as he went on to walk thousands more miles across Africa.
interesting_fact_1: Hill has a second, closer connection to this walk: she also sculpted three of the figures decorating the Scott Monument, just a few steps from where this statue now stands. Its listing was upgraded from Category B to full Category A in 2002.

name: The Scott Monument
description: Tip your head back and the Gothic spire above you climbs 61.1 metres in pale Binny sandstone - or it would look pale, if 150 years of coal smoke from 'Auld Reekie' hadn't turned it almost black. Built 1840-44, it carries 68 carved statuettes of characters from Walter Scott's novels around its base and up its sides, plus a white marble statue of Scott himself by John Steell. You can climb 287 steps through four viewing platforms for a view over the city. Its architect wasn't a trained architect at all: George Meikle Kemp was a self-taught joiner and draughtsman who entered the 1836 design competition under the pseudonym 'John Morvo', the name of Melrose Abbey's medieval master mason, expecting his lack of credentials to sink his chances.
interesting_fact_1: Kemp won the competition, but never saw his monument finished: walking home from the site on a foggy night in March 1844, he fell into the Union Canal and drowned, just months before the tower's completion.

name: Castle View
address: West Princes Street Gardens, near Ross Bandstand, Edinburgh
description: From the floor of the gardens, tip your head all the way back: Edinburgh Castle sits balanced on a sheer volcanic crag rising straight out of what's now manicured parkland beneath your feet. Castle Rock is the neck of an extinct volcano, hard dolerite formed roughly 340 million years ago. Glaciers later scoured west to east across the landscape, stripping away the softer rock on every side except the sheltered eastern flank - leaving the classic 'crag and tail' shape still visible today: the sheer cliff facing you here, and the long gentle slope of the Royal Mile trailing away behind the fortress on the far side.
interesting_fact_1: The lawn under your feet used to be underwater, and worse. King James III had this hollow flooded around 1460 to create the Nor Loch, a defensive loch guarding the castle's northern approach - which then spent centuries as the Old Town's sewer and, during Scotland's witch-hunting era, its unofficial execution site: more than 300 people were tried for witchcraft on or around its banks, with eleven women reportedly drowned here in a single day in 1624. When engineers drained the loch's western end between 1813 and 1820 to create these gardens, workers dug up a chest containing human skeletons buried in the mud.

name: Old Waverley Hotel
description: This seven-storey Victorian facade across from the gardens and Waverley Station is a building that spent its first quarter-century serving no alcohol at all. Built in 1848 to a design by architect John Armstrong for hotelier Robert Cranston, it opened with 86 rooms, one of the largest hotels on the street at the time. The Cranston family ran it for decades, and their name stuck to the building informally long before 'Old Waverley' became its official one, a nod to the station and the Sir Walter Scott novel it was named after.
interesting_fact_1: For almost 25 years it operated as 'Cranston's Temperance Hotel', the first temperance hotel in Scotland. Robert Cranston was a committed temperance campaigner as well as a hotelier, and his teetotal Princes Street establishment stood as a deliberate statement in a city otherwise thick with taverns and licensed hotels, before the business eventually dropped the policy and became the more conventional hotel operating today.

name: Museum on the Mound
description: Walk into this grand building and you're inside a working bank, not a retired one: this free museum occupies part of the Bank of Scotland's original headquarters, designed by Robert Reid and Richard Crichton and built between 1802 and 1806 for a bank that was already, by then, over a century old - founded in 1695 as Scotland's first bank, and in 1696 the first commercial bank in Europe to issue paper banknotes. Exhibits cover the story of money and banking through historic banknotes, an interactive 1820s life-assurance display, financial crime and security, and raised maps tracing the Old Town's development since the 1600s.

A small predecessor museum here opened as far back as 1986, launched by crime novelist Ian Rankin.
interesting_fact_2: In 2017 the bank announced this museum would close - only to reverse the decision after a public outcry, keeping it open and free to this day.

name: Assembly Hall
description: This neo-Gothic hall sits directly east of Edinburgh Castle atop the Mound, and depending on the month it's either Scotland's most solemn church gathering or one of the Fringe's busiest stages. David Bryce designed it in 1858 for the Free Church of Scotland, formed after the 1843 Disruption split a huge breakaway movement from the established Church, and it has served since 1929 as the meeting place for the General Assembly of the Church of Scotland. Between 1999 and 2004 it took on another role entirely, hosting the newly reconvened Scottish Parliament while the purpose-built Holyrood building was under construction.
interesting_fact_1: One of its most significant moments came in 1910, when 1,355 delegates gathered here for the World Missionary Conference, an event widely credited as the starting point of the modern ecumenical movement.

name: Edinburgh City Relief Map
description: Set into the pavement here is a bronze high-relief model of central Edinburgh, reproducing everything from Lothian Road in the west to Regent Road in the east, Queen Street in the north down to the Cowgate in the south - Castle, Calton Hill, Waverley Station and Princes Street Gardens all rendered in raised bronze, with raised lettering naming the major streets. Staff at the Edinburgh branch of Marks & Spencer presented it to the City of Edinburgh in 1984 to mark the company's centenary, but its real purpose is tactile rather than decorative: casting the city in high relief lets visitors with visual impairments explore the shape of Edinburgh's skyline by touch.

name: Duke of Wellington Statue
description: At the eastern tip of Princes Street, Copenhagen rears above the traffic on his hind legs, forever mid-stride toward Waterloo Place, with the Duke seated calm and upright in the saddle. Sir John Steell cast this bronze after winning the commission in 1842, and it was unveiled on 18 June 1852 - the 37th anniversary of Waterloo itself - directly in front of General Register House. Wellington, then 83 and in his final months, couldn't attend, but veterans who'd served under him turned out anyway. Copenhagen was no invented prop: this was the real horse Wellington rode through the whole Waterloo campaign, kept in comfortable retirement afterwards until he died in 1836 aged 28, and buried with full military honours.
interesting_fact_1: Wellington himself was too frail at 83 to attend his own statue's unveiling, but veterans who had fought under him at Waterloo showed up for the ceremony anyway.
interesting_fact_3: In 2026 the statue started making the news for the wrong reason: photographed wearing a traffic cone, a decades-old Glasgow tradition that spread to Edinburgh's own statues during the World Cup and that city councillors have publicly called 'undignified'.

name: General Register House
description: The pale stone facade closing off the east end of Princes Street is the oldest purpose-built public record office anywhere in Britain or Ireland - one of the oldest of its kind still doing the job it was built for, anywhere in the world. Robert Adam laid its foundation stone on 27 June 1774, but the money kept running out, and it wasn't fully finished until 1788. Step inside for the real reward: the Adam Dome, a soaring rotunda lit only by a central oculus, modelled deliberately on Rome's Pantheon and still the largest domed room Adam ever built, standing 80 feet high.
interesting_fact_1: Adam worked small carved thistles into the dome's otherwise thoroughly Roman anthemion frieze - a quiet Scottish signature slipped into an imported classical language. The building was judged too small almost as soon as it was finished, and architects Robert Reid and Archibald Elliot were called back to extend it and dig further record storage into the basement.

name: The Balmoral Hotel
description: From Waverley Bridge, the Balmoral's clock tower dominates the skyline, 190 feet of red sandstone topped with four clock faces made by Edinburgh jewellers Hamilton & Inches. It opened on 15 October 1902 as the North British Station Hotel, built directly above Waverley Station by the railway company running the trains beneath it, and didn't become 'The Balmoral' until Sean Connery renamed it during a 1991 refurbishment. Check the time here and you're being lied to on purpose: the clock has run three minutes fast since the day it started ticking, a deliberate trick to help travellers dash for their train, corrected only once a year, at midnight on Hogmanay.
interesting_fact_1: The clock's permanent three-minute fib is only ever corrected once a year, at midnight on Hogmanay, for the city's New Year celebrations.
interesting_fact_2: J.K. Rowling finished writing Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows in room 552 here in January 2007, later signing a marble bust in the room with the date and a line from the book; it's now known as the J.K. Rowling Suite.

name: Waverley Bridge
description: Lean on the railing of Waverley Bridge and you're standing on the station roof: Edinburgh Waverley runs directly beneath your feet in the deep valley that used to hold a loch. Engineers Blyth and Westland built this iron-and-stone crossing in 1894-96, one of three parallel bridges - alongside North Bridge and the Mound - thrown across the old loch-bed to link the New Town on one side with the Old Town on the other. Category A listed since 1991, it once let cars and taxis drive straight down ramps into the station concourse below; that vehicle access was closed off in January 2014, leaving the ramps to pedestrians, cyclists and deliveries.

name: Edinburgh Waverley Station
description: From Waverley Bridge, the station barely announces itself - no grand frontage, just entrances dropping away into a valley on three separate sides, because a legal covenant tied to its construction bans building upward here, specifically to protect the view of Arthur's Seat from Princes Street above. Twenty platforms radiate from one huge island beneath a vast glass roof, most recently reglazed with 370,000 square feet of panels between 2010 and 2012. The name came from Sir Walter Scott: the station merged three rival Victorian stations that had grown up in this valley since 1846, and people were informally calling the combined site 'Waverley' after Scott's novels from around 1854, well before it became official.

name: Waverley Market
description: This sunken plaza off Waverley Bridge is actually a roof: the shopping centre below was deliberately built flush with Princes Street's pavement line so it wouldn't block the classic view across to the Castle and the Old Town. A Victorian fruit and vegetable market moved here in 1869 after the growing railway swallowed its old site under North Bridge; that market's iron-and-glass hall, with a rooftop garden once used for entertainment, was demolished in 1973 after closing the previous November. name: Scotsman Steps
description: Climb these 104 steps and every single one is a different marble, quarried from somewhere else on earth - deep green, blush pink, streaked grey - a deliberate piece of art rather than an accident of budget. The stone staircase itself dates to 1899-1902, built inside an octagonal tower as part of the grand new Scotsman newspaper headquarters going up next door, linking North Bridge above down to Market Street and Waverley Station below. For most of the 20th century it was a dark, neglected shortcut, better known for litter and antisocial behaviour than for anything else.
interesting_fact_1: In 2011 Turner Prize-winning artist Martin Creed reclad every step in a different marble for Work No. 1059, a £250,000 permanent artwork commissioned by the neighbouring Fruitmarket Gallery; Creed said climbing it is 'like walking through the world'.

name: The Scotsman Hotel
description: Pink sandstone turrets crowd the skyline above North Bridge - a building designed to be seen: Dunn & Findlay finished it in 1902 as the headquarters of The Scotsman, then Scotland's leading national daily, in a deliberately dramatic Scots Renaissance style. Inside, the operation ran top to bottom - printing presses on the lower floors, editorial staff in the middle, and, in a nod to older ways of moving news fast, a pigeon loft in the attic. Being right beside Waverley Station meant finished papers could reach the trains within minutes of coming off the press.
interesting_fact_1: The oak-panelled Edwardian reception hall survives as the hotel bar, and a Carrara marble staircase still winds up through the building's core, unchanged from the newspaper's day.

name: Jinglin' Geordie
description: Push into this pub on Fleshmarket Close and you're drinking on the spot where the man it's named after actually lived. George Heriot was a 16th and 17th-century Edinburgh goldsmith nicknamed 'Jinglin' Geordie' for the coins that jingled in his pockets as he walked the Old Town - court goldsmith to King James VI and Queen Anne, and wealthy enough to lend both of them serious money. Inside, a long-case clock, stained-glass thistle and saltire windows, and old prints of the city keep that history visible rather than just implied.
interesting_fact_1: When Heriot died in 1624 he left almost his entire fortune to found a hospital school for 'fatherless boys, freemen's sons of the town of Edinburgh' - that bequest became George Heriot's School, still one of the city's best-known independent schools today.

name: Halfway House
description: Squeeze in here and the name makes instant sense: this is reckoned Edinburgh's smallest pub, wedged exactly halfway up the steep flight of steps that make up Fleshmarket Close between Market Street and Cockburn Street. The bar counter fits about four people at a stretch, with a couple more tables and booths squeezed in around it, the walls hung with railway memorabilia that makes sense given how close you are to Waverley Station's platforms just below. It now operates as part of the Old Town Pub Co, one of fifteen Old Town venues run by Bruce Group Scotland, though it still trades and gets reviewed as a genuine independent free house rather than a chain outlet.
interesting_fact_1: It takes cask ale seriously for a pub this small, running four handpumps of rotating guest beers alongside its own house-label Tullibardine malt whisky behind the bar.

name: Fleshmarket Close
address: Market St & Fleshmarket Cl, Edinburgh EH1 1DE
description: Climb this steep, narrow alley from Market Street up toward Cockburn Street and the High Street, and the name tells you exactly what used to happen here: a flesh, or meat, market once ran along the passage, butchers hanging carcasses with blood running down the slope toward the old Nor Loch that filled the valley now occupied by Princes Street Gardens. The market had moved here from beside the Tron Kirk by the late 17th century, and this close remains one of the most-used shortcuts between the railway station and the Old Town today.
interesting_fact_1: It lent its name to Fleshmarket Close, the fifteenth Inspector Rebus novel by Edinburgh crime writer Ian Rankin, published in 2004.
interesting_fact_2: The close long housed the Jinglin' Geordie pub, once a favourite haunt of journalists from the Evening News and The Scotsman, before both papers moved out to Holyrood in 1999.

name: The Booking Office
description: Through the door at 17 Waverley Bridge is the station's own original booking office, built by the North British Railway as Waverley was rebuilt through the 1890s. Passengers bought tickets here until it became the parcels office around 1984, and its timber-panelled counters were cleared out soon after. Grade A listed, and sitting directly above the station concourse as part of Waverley's own roof, the building passed through spells as licensed premises and a restaurant before J D Wetherspoon opened The Booking Office here in March 2016.
interesting_fact_1: The entrance floor carries a replica of the mosaic that once covered the real Victorian booking hall nearby, showing the North British Railway Company's coat of arms; the original, laid between 1892 and 1902, was ripped out along with the old wood-panelled ticket counters in 1970.
interesting_fact_2: Photographs on the walls recall the station's steam-age heyday - the Flying Scotsman at the platform, 1945 refreshment trolleys, and the sleek 1960s Elizabethan express.

name: The Edinburgh Dungeon
description: Head down into the half-underground gloom behind Waverley Station and you're exactly where this attraction wants you: a genuinely sunken row of Category B listed buildings, its vaulted rooms making a fittingly grim setting for what's inside. Vardon Attractions opened it in 2000, and it's now part of Merlin Entertainments, the same company behind the original London Dungeon, taking visitors through roughly 500 years of Scotland's darker history using live actors, sets and special effects rather than static display cases - eleven shows and a ride, staffed by around fifteen actors moving through the building's vaults.
interesting_fact_1: The finale is the Drop Ride to Doom, a free-fall drop staged as a mock execution; a £500,000-plus refit in November 2016 rebuilt the Witch Hunt show around new effects Merlin billed at the time as a world first for the format.

name: City Art Centre
description: Ride the lift up through this nine-storey stone-clad warehouse and you're inside a building that spent its first eight decades moving goods, not art: built in 1899-1902 by the same architects and in the same years as the Scotsman Hotel further up North Bridge, it started as an extension of the newspaper's works before becoming part of Edinburgh's wholesale fruit and vegetable market. The City of Edinburgh Council converted it into a public gallery in 1980, a scheme that won a RIBA Award for Architecture in 1983, with a 1990s expansion opening it out into six full floors of gallery space.
interesting_fact_1: The council's own collection here runs to around 4,800 works of Scottish art from the 17th century to today, including pieces by J.D. Fergusson, Joan Eardley and Eduardo Paolozzi, though with no permanent display what's actually on the walls changes with each exhibition.
interesting_fact_2: A 1961 bequest from Edinburgh resident Jean Watson has quietly funded the bulk of that collection ever since, still shaping what turns up on show today.

name: Metal Thistle Sculpture
description: Outside the Market Street Hotel, a hand-forged metal thistle bends and ripples as if genuinely caught in a gust - heads and leaves rippling sideways, nothing about it standing stiffly upright. Officially titled 'Blawn Wi' The Wind', Scots for 'blown with the wind', it's the work of Edinburgh blacksmith and metalwork artist Kev Paxton, working through his studio ArtFe, who shaped Scotland's national flower mid-gust rather than in its usual heraldic, straight-backed pose, playing on the plant's old reputation for prickly, 'don't mess with me' resilience. It stands on a public footpath, in the middle of a UNESCO World Heritage Site, which turned out to matter more than the sculpting itself.
interesting_fact_1: Getting a permanently sited sculpture fixed into a public footpath here was its own undertaking: architects Leask, who worked alongside Paxton on the installation, described navigating 'the complexities of consents, permits and logistics' needed to place it inside a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

name: Waverley Steps
description: Head down from Princes Street into the station and steel 'tree' columns branch overhead, holding up a frameless glass canopy that only appeared in 2010-2012 - for over a century before that, this broad stairway was open to the sky, and older Edinburgh residents remember it as one of the windiest spots in the city centre, a funnel catching gusts from every direction. The steps themselves opened in 1902 alongside the North British Hotel next door, now the Balmoral, built by the same North British Railway Company that owned them both.
interesting_fact_1: The £7 million rebuild that added the canopy, plus a new escalator and lift for accessibility, had to satisfy tight heritage rules: Waverley is a Grade A listed station inside a UNESCO World Heritage Area, so every part of the new structure needed sign-off before a single glass panel went up.
interesting_fact_2: The steps can still be gated shut at the top today, whenever the station closes for the night.

name: North Bridge
description: Lean on the railing here and you're standing directly above the platforms of Waverley Station, with the turreted Balmoral Hotel, the Palladian front of General Register House, and, across the valley, the unfinished columns of the National Monument and the Nelson Monument on Calton Hill all in view at once. The first North Bridge, built 1763-72, was the crucial first road link between the medieval Old Town and the new Georgian development rising on the ridge to the north - without it, the New Town could never have been built where it stands. That bridge lasted until 1896; the current one, blue ironwork trimmed in red and gold, went up in two stages between 1894 and 1897, engineered to span directly over the station below.
interesting_fact_1: The bridge's ironwork was fabricated by Sir William Arrol & Co, the Glasgow firm also responsible for the Forth Bridge, completed in 1890 as the first major crossing built entirely of steel, and London's Tower Bridge, which opened the same year North Bridge's own construction began, in 1894.
interesting_fact_2: That first bridge nearly didn't survive its own construction: on the evening of 3 August 1769, the south abutment's walls suddenly gave way, killing five people in the collapse. Engineer William Mylne had underestimated how much loose rubble - tipped down this hillside from the New Town's own foundations - the bridge's footings would have to bear. It's a story that echoes elsewhere on this route: a fish-and-chip shop, a shopping arcade and a boutique cinema built along this same crossing all still tell their own version of it.

name: The Doric Bar

Downstairs, a traditional bar stocks more than fifty single malt whiskies; upstairs, a bistro has been serving fresh, locally sourced food cooked to order for decades, a split-level format that lets it run as both a proper local and a serious dining room.
interesting_fact_1: The name likely nods to 'Doric', the term for the broad dialect of North-East Scotland - and, perhaps coincidentally, to the plainest and sturdiest of the three classical orders of Greek architecture.

name: The Scotsman's Lounge
description: The Scotsman's Lounge is a pub that's been pouring drinks on Cockburn Street since 1860, one of the older continuously running pubs on this stretch of the Old Town, a couple of minutes' walk from the Royal Mile. A small stage keeps live musicians playing most evenings, and the bar carries a large range of malt whiskies alongside the usual pints, under a ceiling papered with autographed banknotes left by visitors from around the world and walls hung with old photographs of pipers and vanished Edinburgh streets.
interesting_fact_1: When the pub reopened after a Covid-era hitch over its outdoor seating in April 2021, Edinburgh council leader Adam McVey issued a public welcome for its return - a small sign of how much these independent Cockburn Street venues matter to the area's identity.
