name: Cockburn Street
description: The curve of the street pulls your eye upward: sandstone tenements rising in a gentle S-bend down toward Waverley, carved here and there with a small monogram, 'PK', if you know where to spot it. You're walking on a street that didn't exist until 1856, when engineers sliced a whole new shortcut straight through a knot of medieval closes to link the Royal Mile with the railway station below. It's named for Henry, Lord Cockburn, a judge celebrated for campaigning to protect Edinburgh's old buildings — a little ironic, since building his namesake street meant bulldozing straight through several of them. These days the serpentine curve is known for something Lord Cockburn probably never predicted: a run of independent, alternative and gothic-leaning boutiques that made Cockburn Street Edinburgh's unofficial home of subculture shopping.
interesting_fact_1: The street's gentle S-curve and shallow gradient (about 1-in-14) were deliberately engineered to ease the climb from Waverley Station up to the Old Town for horses and carriages — fittingly, it's named after Henry, Lord Cockburn, an early champion of preserving Edinburgh's historic buildings, even though building the street destroyed large sections of several medieval closes.

name: Craig's Close
description: Squeeze into Craig's Close and the walls close in fast: this is the narrowest of the surviving original lanes off the Royal Mile, tight enough in places to touch both sides at once. In the 1700s, a tavern here called the Isle of Man Arms hosted the Cape Club, a drinking society whose members took mock-chivalric titles — 'Sir Precenter', 'Sir Forgetful' — and were inducted with a raised fire-poker over a solemn oath, every meeting wound up strictly before 1am, no gambling allowed. The poet Robert Fergusson drank here as 'Sir Precenter'; so did a far less respectable member, Deacon William Brodie, Edinburgh's own double life split between respectable cabinetmaker and city councillor by day and burglar by night, a real case that helped inspire Robert Louis Stevenson's Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde.
interesting_fact_1: A tavern in the close, the Isle of Man Arms, was the meeting place of the 18th-century Cape Club, whose members took satirical knightly titles and were inducted with a raised fire-poker; one member, Deacon William Brodie — respectable cabinetmaker and city councillor by day, burglar by night — had a double life that partly inspired Stevenson's Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde.

name: Old Fishmarket Close
description: Walk into Old Fishmarket Close and you're following a slope fish once tumbled down for three centuries: the close took its name from the market that operated here, first recorded in council minutes in 1539. Stand still and picture 1573, when government cannon battered the High Street during the 'Lang Siege' — the story goes that fish were sent flying clean out of the market stalls onto the surrounding rooftops, with hungry townsfolk scrambling up after them. A grimmer record: in April 1585, a girl working in this close became the first person in Edinburgh recorded to die when plague reached the city. And in 1705, in one of the close's flats, a Dutchman named Abraham Sever kept a pet elephant, nicknamed the 'Dundee Elephant', as a lodger in a medieval Edinburgh tenement.
interesting_fact_1: During the 'Lang Siege' of 1573, cannon fire is said to have blown fish from the close's market stalls onto the surrounding rooftops; just over a decade later, in April 1585, a girl working here became the first recorded plague death when the disease reached Edinburgh.

name: Anchor Close
description: Duck into Anchor Close and you're standing where the modern reference book was born: a small print shop here, run by William Smellie, produced the first-ever edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica in the 1770s. Smellie also printed the first Edinburgh edition of Robert Burns's poems in 1787, and Burns himself spent hours in this close correcting the proofs. The two men's friendship ran to less scholarly pursuits too: Smellie founded a drinking club, the Crochallan Fencibles, which met at the Anchor Tavern here under landlady Fanny Douglas, and it was for this club's private amusement that Burns wrote his most explicit collection of verse, The Merry Muses of Caledonia, kept unpublished and passed around in manuscript for decades because it was considered far too indecent for print.
interesting_fact_1: The club's name was itself a mock-militia joke: 'Crochallan' borrowed a Gaelic cattle-droving song title favoured by landlord Daniel Douglas, bolted onto 'Fencibles', the name for real home-defence militia regiments — members even held parody military ranks, with founder William Smellie serving as the club's self-styled 'colonel'.

name: Tron Kirk Market
description: The clock on the Tron's stone steeple is the timepiece that, for generations, the whole city set its New Year by. Crowds used to pack the High Street outside to hear the Tron's bells ring in Hogmanay at midnight, long before Princes Street Gardens took over as the official party. The church itself was built in the 1630s and 40s, and takes its name from the 'tron', the public weighing beam that once stood outside it, used to check traders weren't short-changing customers in the market that gathered here. It survived as a working parish church until 1952, when a shrinking, depopulated Old Town could no longer support a congregation, and it sat empty for decades before an unlikely second life: today, restored, it houses a market of independent designers and makers, trading resuming, just without the beam.
interesting_fact_1: Crowds traditionally gathered outside the Tron to hear its bells and count down to midnight on Hogmanay, before Princes Street Gardens became Edinburgh's main New Year focus.

name: The Milkman
description: The shopfront still has timber shutters that still slide down into slots below the window, an original feature from when this was a confectioner's shop, part of a row built in 1859 to unify Cockburn Street's newly cut frontage. The hand-painted lettering on the fascia dates back just as far, carefully restored rather than replaced when the current coffee shop moved in. The Milkman opened here in 2015, its name borrowed from the founder's great-grandfather, the last horse-drawn milkman working in the small Aberdeenshire town of Huntly, a nod to a much older, slower way of delivering something good to your door, now reworked as flat whites instead of milk bottles.
interesting_fact_1: The shopfront's timber shutters, which still slide down into slots beneath the window, are original features from the building's 1859 construction as a confectioner's shop, and the cafe's own name honours the founder's great-grandfather, the last horse-drawn milkman in the Aberdeenshire town of Huntly.

name: Sir Chris Hoy Gold Post Box
description: That ordinary-looking pillar box on the corner isn't red because it was never meant to blend in: it's gold, and it's stayed that way since the summer of 2012. Royal Mail repainted a postbox gold in the hometown of every British athlete who won an Olympic gold medal at London 2012, and Edinburgh's track cyclist Sir Chris Hoy won two, so the city got two gold boxes. This one, in Hunter Square, marks his win in the men's Keirin. Look closely and you'll still find the sprint medal's twin marker across town at Hanover Street and Princes Street, a quiet piece of 2012 nostalgia hiding in plain sight on an otherwise unremarkable street corner.
interesting_fact_1: Hoy's two London 2012 golds weren't even his best Games: at Beijing 2008 he won three — team sprint, keirin and individual sprint — the first British man to take three golds at a single Olympics since 1908, and still Scotland's most successful Olympian outright.

name: Old Saint Paul's Scottish Episcopal Church
description: Head down the steep steps off Jeffrey Street and you drop straight into a hidden nave, tucked below street level, lit by dim stained glass rather than daylight. The congregation here traces itself back to 1689, when the last bishop of St Giles', Alexander Rose, refused to accept Presbyterian church government and led his followers out to worship instead in a converted wool store down nearby Carrubber's Close. From there, this Episcopalian congregation became entangled in Scotland's most dangerous politics: many members backed the Jacobite risings of 1715 and 1745, and paid for it, harassed and persecuted under law for decades, only shaking off their reputation for treason after the death of Bonnie Prince Charlie himself in 1788. The current building, finished in 1883, has since been extended twice, its length now three times the original.
interesting_fact_1: The congregation began in 1689 when Bishop Alexander Rose left St Giles' rather than accept Presbyterian church government, worshipping instead in a converted wool store down Carrubber's Close - and as a Jacobite-leaning Episcopalian congregation, its members were later caught up in the 1715 and 1745 risings, with their places of worship persecuted under law for decades afterward.

name: Margaret Tait Filmmaker Plaque
description: Pause here for a name easy to miss among North Bridge's grander landmarks: Margaret Tait, one of Scotland's most singular filmmakers, commemorated for a career the mainstream mostly ignored while she was alive to see it. Tait trained first as a doctor, served in the Royal Army Medical Corps during the Second World War, then went to Rome to study filmmaking before returning to Scotland to make what she called 'film poems', short, intensely observed studies of ordinary life and place, largely self-funded because the British film establishment showed little interest. She didn't direct her first and only feature film, Blue Black Permanent, until 1992, at the age of 74, making her the first Scottish woman to direct a feature-length film, recognition that arrived only after decades spent almost entirely outside the industry she quietly outlasted.
interesting_fact_1: Tait trained as a doctor and served in the Royal Army Medical Corps in WWII before studying filmmaking in Rome and returning to Scotland to make self-funded short 'film poems' - and she didn't direct her only feature film, Blue Black Permanent, until 1992 at age 74, making her the first Scottish woman to direct a feature-length film.

name: The Scotsman Picturehouse
description: Inside the Scotsman Hotel, tucked into what used to be a disused room, are red leather armchairs, individual table lamps and Edwardian cornicing wrapped around one of Edinburgh's smallest cinemas. The building above you is the real story: a 190-foot tower raised in the early 1900s as the grand headquarters of The Scotsman newspaper, marking a triumphant new entrance to the Old Town after North Bridge itself was rebuilt in 1897 - its own construction history, including a genuine disaster, is told at the North Bridge stop on this route. The Scotsman printed the news from this tower for ninety years, until the paper moved out in 1999 and the building was reborn, first as a hotel, then as this boutique picture house.
interesting_fact_1: The building was purpose-built in the early 1900s as The Scotsman newspaper's headquarters, a 190-foot tower that served as the paper's home for ninety years until 1999.

name: O'Neill's Bar
description: Notice how orderly Hunter Square feels compared to the tangle of closes just off it: that's because, unlike almost everything around it, this square wasn't grown over centuries, but planned. It was laid out in the 1780s as part of the hugely controversial South Bridge Improvement Scheme, a project so fiercely opposed it was delayed for a decade before finally demolishing entire wynds of housing and workshops to make way for South Bridge and the streets around it, many of the displaced residents were tenants who received no compensation at all for losing their homes. This particular building on the square has swapped identities more recently too: for years it traded as the Tron Bar before a 2025 renovation turned it into this Irish-themed O'Neill's, its Georgian facade kept largely intact even as everything behind it was stripped out and refitted.
interesting_fact_1: Hunter Square was laid out in the 1780s as part of the South Bridge Improvement Scheme, a deeply controversial project that demolished entire wynds of housing (many displaced tenants received no compensation) - and this particular building traded for years as the Tron Bar before reopening as O'Neill's in 2025.

name: The Inn on the Mile
description: Giant Doric columns hold up this building's portico - a bank dressed as a temple, a favourite architectural trick of the early 20th century, meant to tell customers their money was safe with people who took themselves very seriously indeed. Built in 1923 as a branch of the British Linen Bank, one of Scotland's oldest banking houses, chartered in 1746 originally to finance the country's linen trade, the building later passed to the Bank of Scotland after a 1970s takeover, before finally being stripped of ledgers and counters altogether and reborn as a boutique hotel and pub. High ceilings, cornicing and the sheer scale of the rooms all still whisper 'bank' underneath the beer taps.
interesting_fact_1: The building was constructed in 1923 as a branch of the British Linen Bank, one of Scotland's oldest banks, originally chartered in 1746 to finance the linen trade - it later passed to the Bank of Scotland after a 1970s takeover before being converted into today's hotel and pub.

name: Landy's Fish and Chips
description: The width of the room around you gives away a building shaped by disaster: this stretch of North Bridge only exists because of a full rebuild in 1897, after the original 1763 bridge suffered a dramatic construction accident - the full story is told at the North Bridge stop on this route. The chippy itself is a much newer arrival: opened in late 2024 by the Vittoria Group, an Edinburgh-Italian restaurant family that's been frying in Leith since 1970, it's now run by the third generation, serving classic seaside fish and chips in a two-floor, nautical-themed space a world away from the tenements and workshops that once crowded this exact spot.
interesting_fact_1: The Vittoria Group has been frying fish in Leith since 1970 and is now run by the third generation of the same family - Landy's, opened in 2024, is one of their newest sites, built inside a two-floor space with a deliberately nautical theme.

name: Radisson Blu Hotel
address: The Royal Mile, 80 High St, Edinburgh EH1 1TH, UK
description: Notice how this building manages to look old without actually being old: no fake weathering, no pastiche shopfronts, just traditional Scottish materials and proportions wrapped around a thoroughly modern hotel. It opened in 1990, designed by Scottish architect Ian Begg specifically to fill what was, for years, a conspicuous gap site on the Royal Mile's historic frontage. Begg's solution was a quiet architectural statement: rather than building something overtly modern or trying to fake a genuine historic tenement, he built new in an unashamedly 'Scottish vernacular' style, turrets, small windows, thick stone walls, betting that Edinburgh's Old Town character comes from a way of building, not simply from age. Whatever you make of the result, it's one of very few 20th-century buildings on the Mile trying to speak the same architectural language as its centuries-older neighbours.
interesting_fact_1: The hotel, opened in 1990, was designed by architect Ian Begg to fill a long-standing gap site on the Royal Mile's historic frontage - rather than imitating an old tenement or building overtly modern, he designed it in a deliberately 'Scottish vernacular' style, new construction speaking the same architectural language as its centuries-old neighbours.

name: Carrubber's Close
description: Carrubber's Close is a passage documented since before 1513, one of the oldest lanes on the Mile. After Presbyterians took control of the Church of Scotland in 1690, Episcopalians here had nowhere legal left to worship, so they met in secret in a small chapel down this close, using a wooden altar built to fold flat and vanish if the authorities came looking. Among the students who worshipped here in secret during the 1750s was an American, Samuel Seabury, who later became the first bishop of the Episcopal Church in the United States, a direct line from a hidden altar in an Edinburgh close to the founding of an American religious institution. By the 1880s the close's character had shifted from concealment to conversion: evangelist Dwight L. Moody helped raise the funds to build the Carrubbers Close Mission, whose building still stands here today.
interesting_fact_1: During the 17th and 18th centuries, Episcopalians worshipped secretly in a small chapel down this close, using a wooden altar built to fold away quickly if the authorities came looking - among the students who worshipped there in secret in the 1750s was Samuel Seabury, an American who later became the first bishop of the Episcopal Church in the United States.

name: North Bridge Arcade
address: 7 North Bridge, Arcade, Edinburgh EH1 1QL, UK
description: Through this doorway, the Royal Mile's noise drops away almost instantly: you're inside a covered Victorian shopping arcade, one of only five left standing in the whole of Scotland. Built in 1900, it still has its original bowed shopfront windows, coffered ceiling and a stained-glass dome overhead, all designed to let daylight flood a passage that otherwise runs, tunnel-like, between North Bridge and Cockburn Street. It opened in the same building boom that gave Edinburgh its rebuilt North Bridge in 1897 - a bridge with its own dramatic backstory, told at the North Bridge stop on this route.
interesting_fact_1: The arcade's stained-glass dome and bowed shopfront windows are original to 1900 and rare survivors: only five Victorian shopping arcades like this are still standing anywhere in Scotland.

name: Bishop's Close
address: 129 High St, Bishop's Cl, Edinburgh EH1 1SG, UK
description: Bishop's Close marks where, in 1742, one of the most consequential, and controversial, Scots of the 18th century was born: Henry Dundas, later Viscount Melville, whose statue still towers over St Andrew Square. Dundas rose to become one of the most powerful men in the British government, effectively running Scotland's political patronage for decades. But he's remembered today mostly for something else: as Home Secretary in 1792, he proposed a 'gradual' rather than immediate abolition of the slave trade, a delay historians still argue over — critics say it held up abolition until 1807, prolonging the trade's toll by hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans; defenders say abolition would have stalled regardless. The debate is very much alive: Edinburgh City Council added a plaque addressing his slavery links to his statue as recently as 2021.
interesting_fact_1: Henry Dundas, later Viscount Melville, was born in Bishop's Close in 1742 and went on to control much of Scotland's political patronage in the late 18th century - as Home Secretary in 1792 he proposed delaying rather than immediately abolishing the slave trade, a decision historians still dispute the true impact of; Edinburgh City Council added an explanatory plaque to his statue in St Andrew Square in 2021.

name: The Mitre Bar
description: The name above the door is a clue to something buried underneath your feet: in 1615, this spot was home to a grand tenement belonging to John Spottiswood, then Bishop of St Andrews, and the pub's mitre, a bishop's ceremonial headdress, nods directly to him. That original building burned down in 1814, and the tavern that replaced it kept the bishop's memory alive in name only, or so the story goes: locals still claim his throne lies buried somewhere beneath the current bar, and that his ghost hasn't quite left the building either. Whether or not you believe the haunting, the Mitre's dim lighting, packed bookshelves and old prints of the city make it easy to imagine a 17th-century bishop feeling right at home.
interesting_fact_1: The pub takes its name and symbol, a bishop's mitre, from John Spottiswood, Bishop of St Andrews, whose tenement stood on this site in 1615 before burning down in 1814 - local legend holds that his throne is buried beneath the current bar, and that his ghost still walks the pub.

name: Bailie Fyfe's Close
description: The mouth of Bailie Fyfe's Close, looking east along the High Street, sits at the western edge of one of Edinburgh's deadliest nights. On 24 November 1861, an ancient seven-storey tenement between here and neighbouring Paisley Close suddenly gave way in the night, its decayed timbers unable to bear the weight of up to a hundred residents; 35 people died in the rubble. As rescuers worked through the wreckage, a boy's voice rang out from beneath the debris: 'Heave awa', lads, I'm no' deid yet!' He survived, and his defiant cry was carved into the replacement building next door at Paisley Close, above a sculpted likeness of his face, that close now nicknamed the 'Heave Awa' Hoose'. The close itself is named after Gilbert Fyfe, a merchant and city 'bailie' who lived here in the 1680s; later residents included the young Francis Jeffrey, future founder of the Edinburgh Review.
interesting_fact_1: On 24 November 1861, a seven-storey tenement standing between this close and neighbouring Paisley Close collapsed in the night, killing 35 people - a boy trapped in the rubble was heard shouting 'Heave awa', lads, I'm no' deid yet!', and he survived, his cry later carved onto the replacement building at Paisley Close next door, nicknamed the 'Heave Awa' Hoose'.

name: The Nutcracker Christmas Shop
description: Push open the door and you're hit immediately by pine and spice: this small, family-run shop keeps Christmas running all year on a street that has, in various forms, sold goods to passing trade for hundreds of years. Inside, hand-carved German nutcrackers stand shoulder to shoulder with baubles and room fragrances sourced from around the world, continuing a long Royal Mile tradition of tightly packed specialist shops squeezed into narrow tenement frontages, each one making the most of just a few feet of street-level space. It's a reminder that behind the grand history of closes and clubs and kirks that line this street, ordinary retail, someone trying to sell you something useful, or at least sparkly, has been happening here for just as long.
interesting_fact_1: The shop is part of Nutcracker Christmas Co., a small family-run business with sister shops in York and St Andrews.

name: Netherbow Wellhead
description: Brass markers are set into the pavement around this monument: they trace the exact footprint of the Netherbow Port, the great fortified gateway that once stood here and formed the true edge of medieval Edinburgh. Anyone passing through it had to pay a toll, even residents, and the poor who couldn't afford it were effectively trapped on one side or the other, which is how this spot earned its enduring nickname, 'World's End': to those who could never afford to leave, the gate really did mark where their known world stopped. The gate itself, rebuilt in 1571, was demolished in 1764 as the city outgrew its walls, but the wellhead beside it survived: designed by Sir William Bruce and built around 1685 by master mason Robert Mylne, it once fed drinking water piped in from burns south of the town to six wells along the High Street.
interesting_fact_1: The Netherbow Port toll gate once stood here, marking the true edge of medieval Edinburgh; the poor who couldn't afford its toll were effectively trapped on one side, giving the area its nickname 'World's End' - the gate was demolished in 1764, but the surviving wellhead beside it was designed by Sir William Bruce and built around 1685 by master mason Robert Mylne, supplying piped drinking water to the High Street.

name: The Albanach
description: The name above the door is the giveaway: 'Albanach' is simply Gaelic for 'Scotsman' or 'Scottish person', a bold, no-nonsense title for a pub sitting on the Royal Mile a short walk from the old Netherbow gate, historically the boundary where medieval Edinburgh itself ended. Inside, the pub backs onto the top of Fleshmarket Close, and its rear windows look straight down that steep lane toward Market Street below, a genuine slice of Old Town topography you can take in with a pint in hand. True to its name, the bar stocks over 220 Scottish malt whiskies, making the case for its Gaelic title one dram at a time.
interesting_fact_1: 'Albanach' is Gaelic for 'Scotsman' or 'Scottish person' - the pub's rear restaurant windows look directly down Fleshmarket Close toward Market Street below, and true to its name, it stocks more than 220 Scottish malt whiskies.

name: The Advocate
description: You're standing in Hunter Square, a rare piece of planned geometry dropped into Edinburgh's tangled Old Town, laid out in the 1780s as part of the fiercely contested South Bridge Improvement Scheme, a project so unpopular it was delayed a decade before finally flattening entire wynds of housing to build South Bridge and the streets around it. This particular pub has worn several names over the years, most memorably 'Fiscal & Firkin' before rebranding as the Advocate, a nod to the square's proximity to the courts and to St Giles' Cathedral just around the corner, where the city's lawyers still put in a full day's work before some of them wander over here for an evening pint.
interesting_fact_1: Hunter Square was laid out in the 1780s as part of the controversial South Bridge Improvement Scheme, which demolished entire wynds of older housing - the pub itself was previously known as the 'Fiscal & Firkin' before its rebrand to The Advocate, a nod to its proximity to the law courts around St Giles' Cathedral.

name: Malt Shovel Inn
description: Head down to the foot of Cockburn Street and you're standing in a pub that predates the street around it: the Malt Shovel was already trading here in 1800, more than half a century before Cockburn Street itself was carved through the Old Town in the 1850s to link up with Waverley Station. Behind the bar, a wooden gantry in ornate Robert Adam-style baroque, lined with mirrors, backs a serious whisky collection: more than fifty single malts, alongside real ales and the kind of framed old photographs of Edinburgh that turn up in every pub on this stretch of street. Sitting right on the border between the Old and New Towns, a few paces from the station, it's been catching travellers passing between the two halves of the city for longer than the street itself has existed.
interesting_fact_1: The pub was already established in 1800, predating Cockburn Street itself, which wasn't built until the 1850s - it stocks over 50 single malt whiskies behind a wooden gantry in ornate Robert Adam-style baroque design.

name: The Piper's Rest
description: Tucked just behind the Tron, in the same planned square as several other pubs carved out of the 1780s South Bridge development, the Piper's Rest leans hard into a kind of Scottishness other Hunter Square bars only gesture at: dark wood, low light, malt whisky and gin lined up behind the bar, and live traditional music seven nights a week mixing old tunes with newer covers. It's a reminder that Hunter Square itself, despite feeling like an ancient huddle of Old Town buildings, is a relatively late arrival on the Royal Mile's timeline, laid out after 1786 once the controversial South Bridge scheme had finished clearing away the wynds that stood here before.
interesting_fact_1: The pub features live traditional Scottish music seven nights a week.

name: Royal Mile
description: You won't find 'Royal Mile' on a single street sign - it's a Victorian nickname, coined in the late 19th century, for a chain of streets that has no official name of its own. Walking downhill from the Castle to Holyroodhouse, the same road changes its name four times: Castlehill, then Lawnmarket, then High Street - the stretch you're on now - then Canongate. The name comes from the royal processional route once ridden between the two, and the distance really does work out to almost exactly one mile.
interesting_fact_1: Branching off both sides of this street are more than 250 closes - narrow medieval alleyways, most named after a memorable resident or trade rather than assigned a number, since the tightly packed Old Town never had room for conventional street addressing. Many still carry names centuries old, even where the building behind them has been rebuilt many times over.
interesting_fact_2: The Old Town's severe overcrowding here - whole extended families packed into single rooms up tenements that were the tallest in Europe at the time - had a hidden cost: the Great Fire of 1824 tore through this district for five days, killed at least ten people, and destroyed so much that swathes of what you're walking past now date only from the Victorian rebuild that followed.
interesting_fact_3: In 1561, a nineteen-year-old Mary, Queen of Scots rode up this exact street for the first time after eighteen years in France, to a coronation-scale welcome - the start of a reign that would end, seven years later, in her forced abdication.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: Adam Smith Statue
description: Ten feet of bronze, wrapped in a toga-like gown,, gazing down the High Street with a rolled scroll in hand. This is Adam Smith, the economist who lived a few closes from here and worked as a customs commissioner just down the road, writing much of 'The Wealth of Nations' between Old Town coffeehouses. Smith is usually cast as capitalism's patron saint, so it's easy to miss that he was also fiercely quoted by 18th and 19th-century abolitionists as an opponent of slavery. When Edinburgh Council reviewed its public statues for links to slavery and empire after 2020, this one was examined and cleared - the man behind 'the invisible hand' turns out to have been one of his era's clearer voices against human bondage.
interesting_fact_1: Despite his reputation as capitalism's figurehead, Smith was frequently cited in anti-slavery literature and was reviewed - and cleared - by Edinburgh's 2020 Slavery and Colonialism Legacy Review Group; he is buried a short walk from here in Canongate Kirkyard, near his old home at Panmure House.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: Mercat Cross
description: A unicorn balances on its column above the spot where Edinburgh once did its shouting. The Mercat Cross - first recorded in a charter of 1365 - was the city's marketplace, its news-stand, and its stage for royal proclamations: elections, coronations and the deaths of monarchs were all bellowed from this platform. It had a darker use too. The square around it doubled as an execution site, where high-status prisoners met 'the Maiden', Edinburgh's own guillotine. The current cross is a rebuild dating largely from 1617, its octagonal base a gift from Prime Minister William Gladstone in 1885. Official proclamations - a new monarch's accession, for instance - are still read here today, an unbroken link to a 660-year-old tradition of turning stone into news.
interesting_fact_1: First recorded in a charter of 1365, the present cross was rebuilt in 1617 and given its octagonal base in 1885, paid for by Prime Minister William Gladstone - the square beside it also doubled as an execution site for high-status prisoners, killed on a guillotine nicknamed 'the Maiden'.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: Edinburgh City Chambers
description: Walk into the courtyard behind that grand colonnaded facade and you're standing on top of a buried street. Edinburgh City Chambers began life in 1760 as the Royal Exchange, built by Lord Provost George Drummond to drag the city's merchants off the crowded High Street and into a purpose-built trading hall. But the site had a problem: an entire close, Mary King's Close, ran underneath it. Rather than clear it fully, the builders lopped off the tops of the buildings and built straight over them, sealing families' homes and workshops below street level. The last resident wasn't evicted until 1902, during a further extension. What was buried in a fit of civic improvement is now one of Edinburgh's strangest visitor attractions, reached by a stair a few steps from where you're standing.
interesting_fact_1: Built in 1760 as the Royal Exchange, designed by John Adam, to move merchants off the crowded High Street and into an indoor trading hall - it was constructed directly over sealed-off closes, including Mary King's Close, whose last resident was only removed in 1902.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: Real Mary King's Close
description: Peer down this close and you're looking at a street Edinburgh tried to forget. In 1645, plague tore through the Old Town, killing more than half the population in places, and Mary King's Close - narrow, cramped and packed with tenement dwellers - was hit hardest. Legend holds that around 300 infected residents were bricked in and left to die, though historians now think the truth is messier: the close was simply abandoned as families fled or perished, its rooms left standing as they were. When the Royal Exchange was built over the site in the 1750s, builders truncated the buildings rather than demolish them, burying entire houses intact. Named for a 17th-century fabric merchant, the close stayed hidden underground for centuries until it reopened in 2003 as one of the only places in the world where you can walk through a genuine 17th-century street.
interesting_fact_1: The close is named after Mary King, a merchant burgess who lived there in the 1630s - buried beneath the Royal Exchange (now City Chambers) since the 1750s, it reopened to visitors as The Real Mary King's Close in 2003.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: Parliament House
description: This is the room where Scotland argued with itself. Parliament House was built in 1640, funded by subscriptions from Edinburgh's own citizens, and is thought to be the world's first building constructed purely to house a parliament. Scotland's parliament sat here until the 1707 Act of Union dissolved it, and the hall was later absorbed into what is now the Supreme Courts of Scotland - so lawyers, not politicians, pace its length today. There's a very Edinburgh postscript: in 2006, ahead of a 58 million pound refurbishment, the Scottish Government asked the city council who actually owned the building. The council admitted it didn't know. Ownership was untangled only after government lawyers dug through the archives, more than 350 years after the first stone was laid.
interesting_fact_1: Completed in 1640 and thought to be the world's first purpose-built parliament building; Scotland's parliament sat here until the 1707 Act of Union.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: St Giles' Cathedral
description: The spire shaped like a crown is 15th-century propaganda in stone - a deliberate echo of the Crown of Scotland kept up at the Castle. St Giles' has stood on this site since 1124, though most of what you see dates from the 14th to 16th centuries. It has been battled over as much as prayed in: in 1385 an English army was sent north specifically to burn it down, and scorch marks from that attack reportedly stayed visible on the pillars into the 19th century. Its most famous moment of violence came from one furious woman: in 1637, when a new prayer book was forced on the congregation, a local trader named Jenny Geddes allegedly hurled her stool at the preacher's head, sparking a riot that helped ignite the Covenanting wars. And despite the name everyone uses, it hasn't technically been a cathedral since the 17th century - officially, it's the High Kirk of Edinburgh.
interesting_fact_1: The crown-shaped spire, dating from the 15th century, is modelled on the Crown of Scotland, still on display at Edinburgh Castle - and despite its name, the building has not officially been a cathedral since the 17th century, its formal title being the High Kirk of Edinburgh.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: Signet Library
description: Inside is a room a king once called the finest drawing room in Europe. The Signet Library, home to the Society of Writers to the Signet - Scotland's oldest legal society, founded in 1594 - was completed in 1822 with a lower library of pale columns and gilded galleries, and an upper library of fluted Corinthian columns beneath a coffered dome. When George IV visited Edinburgh that same year, the first royal visit to Scotland in nearly two centuries, he used the Upper Library as a reception room before a banquet held in his honour in the neighbouring Parliament Hall. Two centuries of Scottish legal paperwork - deeds, wills, the machinery behind land ownership across the country - have passed through the hands of the Writers to the Signet who still work here today.
interesting_fact_1: George IV called the library 'the finest drawing room in Europe' after visiting in 1822 during his famous state visit to Edinburgh - it's home to the Society of Writers to the Signet, founded in 1594 and Scotland's oldest legal society.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: Heart of Midlothian Mosaic
description: The heart-shaped mosaic under your feet marks one of Edinburgh's grimmer addresses. For over 400 years this spot held the Old Tolbooth: a prison, courthouse and site of public executions that loomed over the High Street until it was demolished in 1817. Locals still spit on the heart today, a habit that supposedly began as an act of contempt for the prison rather than a wish for good luck, though most visitors now do it hoping for the opposite. Walter Scott's 1818 novel 'The Heart of Midlothian', named for the same site, was popular enough that Edinburgh's own football club later borrowed the title too - which is why Heart of Midlothian FC's nickname and this pavement mosaic share more than a coincidence of naming.
interesting_fact_1: The mosaic marks the site of the Old Tolbooth, a prison and execution site that stood here for over 400 years until 1817 - spitting on the heart is a genuine local tradition, originally a gesture of contempt for the old prison rather than a wish for luck, and Heart of Midlothian Football Club takes its name from this site too, via Walter Scott's 1818 novel of the same name.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: Brodie's Close
description: This narrow close is where Edinburgh's most notorious double life began. William Brodie - respected cabinet-maker, city councillor, and Deacon of the Wrights and Masons - was born here on the Lawnmarket in 1741, the son of a well-off tradesman. By day he was pious and prosperous; by night, using his professional access to wealthy clients' locks, he pressed their keys into putty, cast duplicates, and burgled their homes with a gang of thieves. The story outlived him by a century: Robert Louis Stevenson, whose own childhood bedroom held furniture Brodie had built, grew up on tales of the deacon's secret life, and many believe Brodie's double existence directly shaped 'The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde'. Brodie himself never saw the book - he was hanged in 1788, on gallows some accounts say he had personally helped redesign.
interesting_fact_1: William Brodie, respected councillor by day and burglar by night, was born in this close in 1741 - Robert Louis Stevenson's family owned furniture made by Brodie, and Brodie's double life is widely credited as an inspiration for 'The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde'; Brodie himself was hanged in 1788, reportedly on a gallows design he had helped improve.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: Deacon Brodies Tavern
description: The pub sign above you shows half respectable gentleman, half shadow - Deacon Brodie's split personality rendered in paint. The real William Brodie was a wealthy 18th-century cabinet-maker and city councillor who spent his nights leading a gang of burglars through Old Town closes, using keys copied from his legitimate locksmith work. The scandal broke in 1788: Brodie fled to Amsterdam, was arrested trying to board a ship for America, brought back to Edinburgh in chains, and hanged before a crowd of around 40,000 - reportedly the largest Edinburgh had seen in living memory. His story became literary gold: Robert Louis Stevenson, who grew up nearby with furniture Brodie had built, is widely thought to have drawn on Brodie's double life when writing 'Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde' a century later. The tavern has traded on his name - and his ghost - ever since.
interesting_fact_1: Brodie fled to Amsterdam after his burglary gang was exposed and was caught trying to board a ship bound for America; brought back to Edinburgh, he was hanged in 1788 before a crowd estimated at 40,000, said to be the largest public gathering the city had seen.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: Statue of Walter Francis Montagu Douglas Scott
description: This bronze figure in ceremonial Garter robes is Walter Francis Montagu Douglas Scott, 5th Duke of Buccleuch and 7th Duke of Queensberry - once one of the largest private landowners in Britain, with estates stretching across the Scottish Borders. Unveiled in 1888 and sculpted by Sir Joseph Edgar Boehm, the statue's plinth carries detailed panels of battle scenes and episodes from his family's history, a reminder that the Buccleuch dukes saw themselves as central figures in Scotland's story, not just its landscape. He served more than thirty years in public office, including as Lord Privy Seal, and helped fund infrastructure across Victorian Scotland. Look closely at the pose: cloak gathered in one hand, gloves in the other, weight on his forward leg - a sculptor's formula for projecting quiet, hereditary authority in bronze.
interesting_fact_1: The Buccleuch dukes were among the largest private landowners in Britain, with estates across the Scottish Borders.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: Robert Burns House Plaque
address: Lady Stair's Close & Lawnmarket, Edinburgh EH1 2NT
description: The plaque above this close marks a small, specific moment: the first time Robert Burns properly arrived in Edinburgh. In 1786, the 27-year-old poet came to the city to arrange the second printing of his poems, having already caused a sensation with his first, self-funded 'Kilmarnock Edition'. He lodged in Baxter's Close, a lane just east of here that was later demolished to build George IV Bridge - so this plaque, on the close beside it, is the nearest fixed point left to where the ploughman-poet first lived among Edinburgh's literary and legal elite, who were soon fawning over him. Within months he had gone from tenant farmer to the toast of the city's drawing rooms, an ascent almost as sudden and dramatic as anything in his poetry.
interesting_fact_1: The plaque commemorates Burns's first visit to Edinburgh in 1786, when he came to arrange a new edition of his poems - his actual lodgings, in the now-demolished Baxter's Close nearby, were cleared to build George IV Bridge.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: Makars' Court
address: Makars' Court, Lady Stair's Close, Edinburgh EH1 2PA
description: As you cross this courtyard, the paving slabs beneath your feet are inscribed with lines from Scottish writers spanning seven centuries. Makars' Court - 'makar' being the old Scots word for a poet or maker - was conceived as a living literary monument, its earliest quotation from 14th-century poet John Barbour and its more recent additions from writers who died within living memory, such as Muriel Spark. The quotations run across Gaelic, Scots, English and Latin, reflecting the different languages Scotland has written in over the centuries. New flagstones are still added periodically, meaning the pavement itself keeps growing - a monument that, unusually, is never quite finished.
interesting_fact_1: 'Makar' is the old Scots word for a poet or literary craftsperson, the origin of the court's name - its inscribed quotations span from 14th-century poet John Barbour to 20th and 21st-century writers like Muriel Spark, in Gaelic, Scots, English and Latin.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: The Writers' Museum
address: Lawnmarket, Lady Stair's Close, Edinburgh EH1 2PA
description: Duck through the door and you're inside a house built in 1622, its stair narrow enough to remind you how small people, and their possessions, once were. Lady Stair's House takes its name from Elizabeth Dundas, Dowager Countess of Stair, who bought the property in 1719; by the 1890s it had fallen into disrepair until the town planner Patrick Geddes persuaded Lord Rosebery to fund its restoration. The house was gifted to the city in 1907 and opened as a museum in 1913, and today it holds relics of Scotland's three literary giants - Robert Burns, Walter Scott and Robert Louis Stevenson - including Burns's own writing desk and the printing press on which Scott's Waverley novels first rolled off.
interesting_fact_1: The house dates from 1622 and was restored in the 1890s after town planner Patrick Geddes intervened to save it from dereliction - its exhibits today include Robert Burns's writing desk and the printing press used for Walter Scott's Waverley novels.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: Alexander and Bucephalus Statue
address: City Chambers Courtyard, High Street, Edinburgh EH1 1DF
description: The horse's ears are worth a closer look before you take in the drama of the scene. This bronze - Alexander the Great taming his wild stallion Bucephalus - was sculpted by John Steell, modelled in 1832 but not cast until 1883, more than fifty years later. It originally stood in St Andrew Square before being moved here in 1916 to make room for the Gladstone Memorial. The oddity is in the details: it's rumoured that when a pay dispute broke out between Steell and the committee funding the piece, the sculptor got his revenge by giving the horse the ears of a pig rather than a stallion - a small, permanent insult cast in bronze and now standing outside the seat of Edinburgh's civic government.
interesting_fact_1: Sculpted by John Steell, modelled in 1832 but not cast in bronze until 1883, a fifty-year gap - it originally stood in St Andrew Square and was relocated here in 1916, and according to local legend, Steell gave the horse pig's ears in retaliation for not being paid in full by the funding committee.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: Hugh Miller Plaque
description: This plaque marks the offices of a newspaper edited by one of Victorian Edinburgh's more unlikely career changes. Hugh Miller began as a stonemason in Cromarty, self-taught and largely self-made, before becoming a serious geologist and writer. From these offices at 297 High Street, between 1840 and 1856, he edited 'The Witness', the newspaper of the Free Church of Scotland, and used its pages to serialise his own geological writing, including 'The Old Red Sandstone' - work now recognised as pioneering in the young science of paleoecology. His life had a dark final chapter: a devout opponent of evolutionary theory on religious grounds, and increasingly troubled by mental illness, Miller took his own life in 1856, just a few years before Darwin's ideas would upend the fossil record he had spent his career studying.
interesting_fact_1: Miller trained as a stonemason before becoming a self-taught geologist and writer, editing 'The Witness' newspaper from these offices between 1840 and 1856 - he serialised his own geological studies, including 'The Old Red Sandstone', in the paper's pages.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: General Stanislaw Maczek Statue
address: City Chambers Courtyard, High Street, Edinburgh EH1 1YJ
description: Sit near this bronze figure for a moment and you're keeping company with a man Poland tried to erase. General Stanislaw Maczek commanded the 1st Polish Armoured Division, which Winston Churchill entrusted with defending Scotland's east coast against invasion during the Second World War. Maczek went on to play a decisive role in the Battle of Normandy, helping close the Falaise Pocket and trap thousands of retreating German troops, then liberated towns across France, Belgium and the Netherlands. But when Poland fell under Communist rule after the war, the regime stripped him of his citizenship as punishment for having served the West. Unable to return home, Maczek settled quietly in Edinburgh and lived here until his death in 1994 at the age of 102.
interesting_fact_1: Maczek commanded the 1st Polish Armoured Division, which helped trap German forces at the Falaise Pocket during the Battle of Normandy - Poland's post-war Communist government later stripped him of his citizenship, and he remained in Edinburgh for the rest of his life, dying here in 1994 aged 102.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: The News Steps
description: 124 steps drop from here to Market Street below, cutting a shortcut between the Old Town and the New that saves you the long way round by North Bridge. The name comes from the newspaper trade: from the 1870s, St Giles Street above you filled with newspaper offices designed by David Bryce, earning it the nickname 'the Fleet Street of Scotland'. Journalists and printers would have hammered up and down these same steps on deadline, moving between the presses and the rest of the city. From partway down you get one of the better under-the-radar views in Edinburgh - North Bridge, Calton Hill, and the gardens of the Bank of Scotland spilling down to your left.
interesting_fact_1: The name comes from the cluster of newspaper offices, designed by architect David Bryce, that stood on St Giles Street from the 1870s - earning the steps the nickname 'the Fleet Street of Scotland' for their newspaper-trade associations.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: Advocate's Close
description: Walk to the mouth of this close and look through the arch - if you time it right, the gap perfectly frames the Scott Monument on Princes Street far below. Advocate's Close drops steeply from the Royal Mile down toward Cockburn Street, its name borrowed from Sir James Stewart, Lord Advocate of Scotland, who lived here from 1635 to 1713. Before that it went by several other names, taken from whichever prominent resident happened to own the property at the time - a common habit in the Old Town, where closes were rebranded generation after generation. Once a fashionable address for gentry and professionals, it lost its top floors in the slum clearances of the 1920s, and today hides a Victorian pump house turned bar behind its stone walls.
interesting_fact_1: Named after Sir James Stewart, Lord Advocate of Scotland, who lived here from 1635 to 1713 - before that it went by several other names, including Cant's Close and Home's Close, after earlier residents, a common pattern for Old Town closes.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: Warriston's Close
description: This close looks unremarkable from the High Street, but step inside and you're standing at the entrance to one of Edinburgh's strangest survivals. Warriston's Close leads down to the sealed, centuries-old streets now open to visitors as The Real Mary King's Close - a warren of 17th-century tenements that were partially built over rather than demolished when the Old Town was redeveloped in the 1750s. In Edinburgh's crowded past, closes like this one could be locked at both ends at night, penning residents in and keeping outsiders out, a reminder of just how tightly controlled - and how vertical - life in the Old Town once was, with buildings rising up to eight storeys above the narrow lane.
interesting_fact_1: Warriston's Close is the modern access point to The Real Mary King's Close, the sealed 17th-century streets beneath the City Chambers - closes like this were often gated and locked at night to control who could pass through.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: Sir Robert W Philip Plaque
description: This modest plaque marks a genuinely world-first moment in medicine. In 1887, near this spot on Bank Street, Dr Robert Philip opened what's recognised as the first dedicated tuberculosis clinic anywhere in the world - two small rooms that became the Victoria Dispensary for Consumption and Diseases of the Chest. Tuberculosis, or consumption, was one of the 19th century's great killers, spreading easily through Edinburgh's cramped, poorly ventilated tenements. Philip's dispensary didn't just treat patients; it pioneered public health education, teaching ordinary Edinburgh residents how to avoid catching and spreading the disease long before antibiotics existed. His model - treatment paired with prevention - spread internationally and eventually grew into the Royal Victoria Hospital.
interesting_fact_1: In 1887, Robert Philip opened the world's first dedicated tuberculosis clinic in two rooms near this spot on Bank Street - his treatment-and-education model for fighting TB was copied internationally and led to his appointment as Edinburgh's first professor of tuberculosis in 1917.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: Stevenlaw's Close
description: This close connects the High Street down to the Cowgate, but its most famous former resident never asked to be famous. James Wilson - known locally as 'Daft Jamie' - lived in Stevenlaw's Close before he was murdered by the West Port killers William Burke and William Hare, who sold bodies to Dr Robert Knox for anatomy lectures. Unlike most of Burke and Hare's other victims, Jamie was a well-known figure around the Old Town, and when his body was recognised on Knox's dissection table, it triggered the public outrage that finally exposed the murders. A gentler resident once lived here too: Allan Masterton, who composed the tunes for several of Robert Burns's songs, including 'Willie Brew'd a Peck o' Maut'.
interesting_fact_1: James Wilson ('Daft Jamie'), a well-known local figure, lived here before being murdered by Burke and Hare and sold to Dr Robert Knox for dissection - composer Allan Masterton, who wrote the music for several Robert Burns songs, also once lived in the close.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: New Assembly Close
description: This close takes its name from the fashionable dancing assemblies that moved here from Old Assembly Close in 1736 and carried on until 1784 - Edinburgh society's answer to a nightclub, minus the music you'd recognise today. When the dancing stopped, the site was rebuilt in 1813 as the head office of the Commercial Bank of Scotland, designed by James Gillespie Graham, and it survived the catastrophic Great Fire of Edinburgh in 1824 that destroyed most of its neighbours. Long after the bank moved out, the building took on a stranger second life: in 1976 it became home to the Edinburgh Wax Museum, meaning a close once devoted to genteel 18th-century courtship later filled up with wax replicas instead.
interesting_fact_1: Named for the Edinburgh Assembly, the city's fashionable dancing society, which met here from 1736 to 1784 - the building later became the head office of the Commercial Bank of Scotland (1813) and survived the Great Fire of Edinburgh in 1824.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: Old Assembly Close
description: Before New Assembly Close existed, this was where Edinburgh came to dance. Old Assembly Close hosted the city's dancing assemblies from 1720, gatherings notable for being run largely by a committee of women - unusual enough at the time that English newspapers reported on it. The assemblies doubled as charity fundraisers for hospitals and good causes, and even inspired early published collections of Scottish dance tunes still played today. The close's luck ran out in 1824, when the Great Fire of Edinburgh tore through the Old Town, destroying four seven-storey tenements here along with the original Assembly Hall itself - one of the worst nights in the city's history, and the reason the close you're standing in now looks so different from its Georgian heyday.
interesting_fact_1: Edinburgh's dancing assemblies were held here from 1720, notably managed by a committee of women, which drew attention even from English newspapers - the Great Fire of Edinburgh in 1824 later destroyed four seven-storey tenements and the original Assembly Hall on this site.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: Borthwick's Close
description: This close has looked narrow, dark and slightly forbidding for close to six centuries, and that's largely by design rather than decay. It takes its name from Lord Borthwick, a lawyer and parliamentarian who built a house here around 1450 specifically to be a short walk from Scotland's Parliament - proof that living near the seat of power has always mattered in Edinburgh. The Borthwicks, related by marriage to Henry VIII, moved in the same circles as the royal courts of both Scotland and England, and later the close also housed Lord Napier of Merchiston, from the family that gave the world logarithms. Today it's easy to miss, tucked between shopfronts, but it still runs through to Tron Square exactly as it always did.
interesting_fact_1: Named after Lord Borthwick, who built a house here around 1450 to be close to the Scottish Parliament - the Borthwick family was related by marriage to Henry VIII, and the close also later housed Lord Napier of Merchiston.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: Statue of James Braidwood
description: This bronze figure, helmet tucked against his thigh, honours the man widely credited as the father of the modern fire service. James Braidwood founded the Edinburgh Fire Brigade in 1824 - the world's first municipal fire service - and pioneered firefighting techniques still taught today, including the idea that firefighters should attack a blaze at its source rather than simply protect nearby buildings. In 1832 he left Edinburgh to establish London's first full-time brigade, a job that eventually killed him: he died in 1861 when a wall collapsed on him while fighting a warehouse fire on Tooley Street, an incident still studied by firefighters. It took until 2008 - nearly 150 years later - for Edinburgh to raise the funds needed for this memorial, unveiled a short walk from where he once served.
interesting_fact_1: Braidwood founded the Edinburgh Fire Brigade in 1824, the world's first municipal fire service - he later founded London's first full-time fire brigade in 1832 and died fighting a fire on Tooley Street in 1861 when a wall collapsed on him.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: The Supreme Courts
description: This is where Scotland's most serious legal business still gets settled. The Supreme Courts of Scotland - the Court of Session for civil cases and the High Court of Justiciary for criminal ones - are both housed inside what began as Parliament House in 1639. The Court of Session dates back even further, created in 1532, making it nearly five centuries old. Behind the Classical facade added in the 1800s lies something visitors rarely see: over 700 rooms spread across seven floors, a genuinely vast legal complex hidden behind what looks, from Parliament Square, like a single grand building. Every working day, advocates in wigs and robes still walk these halls exactly as they have for hundreds of years, making this one of the few places in Edinburgh where the past isn't just commemorated - it's still in active use.
interesting_fact_1: The Court of Session, one of the two Supreme Courts housed here, was created in 1532, making it nearly 500 years old - behind the facade lie more than 700 rooms across seven floors, far larger than the building appears from the square.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: Charles II Statue
description: This is the oldest statue in Edinburgh, and quite possibly the oldest lead equestrian statue anywhere in Britain. Erected in 1685, the very year Charles II died, it shows the king dressed as a Roman emperor, baton in hand, in an artistic shorthand of the era for imperial authority. It cost 2,580 pounds to build, a startling sum for the time, and is thought to be the work of the celebrated Dutch sculptor Grinling Gibbons, better known for his intricate woodcarving in England's grandest houses and churches. More than three centuries of Edinburgh weather have taken their toll: the statue has needed major repairs in 1824, 1922 and again in the 1950s, but it still watches over Parliament Square exactly where it was placed, for a king who never lived to see it unveiled.
interesting_fact_1: Erected in 1685, it is the oldest statue in Edinburgh and possibly the oldest lead equestrian statue in Britain - it is thought to be the work of Dutch sculptor Grinling Gibbons, better known for his ornate woodcarving elsewhere in Britain.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: Roxburgh's Close
description: This close carries the name of a 17th-century cook rather than a nobleman or judge, which sets it apart from most of its grander neighbours. John Roxburgh, made a burgess in 1605, is recorded as owning property here from 1635, and the close was eventually named for him - though it had cycled through several earlier names, including Cant's Close and Cruick's Close, dating back to at least 1578. Its literary claim is quieter but real: several Scottish Gaelic poets made this close their home in the 18th century, writing in a language that was already being pushed to the margins of the very city they lived in. Later redevelopment demolished the buildings separating it from a neighbouring alley, creating the wider Roxburgh Court just beyond.
interesting_fact_1: Named after John Roxburgh, a cook made a burgess in 1605, recorded as living here from 1635 - several Scottish Gaelic-language poets also lived in the close during the 18th century.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: Bank of Scotland
address: Bank of Scotland Private Banking, The Mound, Edinburgh EH1 1YZ, UK
description: That shallow saucer dome crowning the Mound belongs to one of Europe's oldest banks flexing its architectural muscle. Bank of Scotland, founded in 1695, decided at its 100th AGM in 1796 that its directors needed a headquarters worthy of the institution, buying this site from the town council in 1800 for 3,500 pounds. Architects Robert Reid and Richard Crichton, both former pupils of Robert Adam, delivered a domed Georgian villa completed in 1806 that has anchored Edinburgh's skyline for more than two centuries. It still serves as the Scottish headquarters of Lloyds Banking Group today, and part of the building has been turned into the Museum on the Mound, where the vaults and ledgers of three centuries of Scottish banking are on public display.
interesting_fact_1: Bank of Scotland, founded in 1695, is one of the oldest banks still operating in the world - its current headquarters, completed in 1806, was designed by Robert Reid and Richard Crichton, both former pupils of architect Robert Adam.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: Wardrop's Court
address: Wardrop Court, Lawnmarket, Edinburgh EH1 2NY, UK
description: As you pass under the archway, the carved dragons bracketing the entrance aren't original medieval survivors, they're Victorian and Edwardian additions with a personal story behind them. Wardrop's Court took shape in the 1890s when older tenements were cleared to open up the courtyard, on the instructions of town planner Sir Patrick Geddes, who was busy trying to revive Edinburgh's crumbling Old Town rather than bulldoze it. One pair of dragons was carved around 1890 by sculptor J S Gibson; a second pair was carved in 1911 by Arthur Geddes - Patrick's own son - when he was just sixteen, working under a craftsman associated with the Arts and Crafts movement. The clearance to build this court also swept away the house where Robert Burns had stayed on his first visit to the city.
interesting_fact_1: The court's dragon brackets were carved in two phases - around 1890 by J S Gibson, and in 1911 by Arthur Geddes, aged 16, son of town planner Patrick Geddes - the 1890s clearance to create the court also demolished the building where Robert Burns had stayed during his first Edinburgh visit.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: Author's Phrases in the Flagstones
address: Lady Stair's Cl & Makars' Ct, Edinburgh EH1 2LP, UK
description: Slow down here and read what's under your feet. Each flagstone in this courtyard carries a line of Scottish writing, chiselled directly into the stone rather than printed on a plaque - a form chosen deliberately so the words age and weather along with the city itself. The oldest quotation comes from John Barbour, a 14th-century poet whose epic 'The Brus' is one of the earliest surviving works of Scottish literature; more recent stones carry lines from 20th-century writers like Muriel Spark, who died in 2006. The languages shift under your feet as you walk too - Scots gives way to Gaelic, then English, then Latin - a small, physical reminder that Scotland has never had just one literary voice. New stones are still occasionally added, so this pavement counts as a living, growing monument rather than a finished one.
interesting_fact_1: The flagstones are inscribed with quotations spanning from 14th-century poet John Barbour to 20th and 21st-century writers, appearing in four languages - Scots, Gaelic, English and Latin - reflecting Scotland's multilingual literary history.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: Scottish War Poets Memorial
address: Lady Stair's Cl & Makars' Ct, Edinburgh EH1 2LP, UK
description: This grey granite cross, carved with a full-length sword and intricate Celtic knotwork, honours a group of writers who rarely get remembered outside their poems. Unveiled in 2018, almost exactly a century after the Armistice, it commemorates Scottish poets who died in the First World War - men whose words about the trenches are still read, even as their names are far less famous than English contemporaries like Wilfred Owen. The memorial was a genuinely collaborative effort, funded and built through a partnership between universities, the National Library of Scotland, and Edinburgh's own council, and its inscription is as quietly devastating as anything the war poets themselves wrote: 'Sweet be their sleep now wherever they're lying, far though they be from the hills of their home.'
interesting_fact_1: Unveiled in 2018, close to the centenary of the WWI Armistice, to commemorate Scottish poets killed in the First World War - it was funded through a partnership including Edinburgh Napier University, the University of Aberdeen, and the National Library of Scotland.

leg: Tron Kirk Market -> Deacon Brodies Tavern
name: Milne's Court
description: The middle of this square is a genuine piece of urban planning history. Milne's Court was built in 1690 by Robert Mylne, the Royal Master Mason, who bought up and demolished the old tenements and narrow closes that used to clutter this ground, replacing them with something Edinburgh hadn't really seen before: buildings deliberately arranged around an open courtyard, rather than crammed along a slot-like close. It was a small architectural revolution for a city famous for its claustrophobic lanes. The court fell into disrepair over the following centuries, but in the 1960s the University of Edinburgh stepped in, restoring it with donations from local benefactors; it reopened as student accommodation in 1969 and still houses students today, more than three centuries after Mylne first laid it out.
interesting_fact_1: Built in 1690 by Robert Mylne, the Royal Master Mason, it's considered Edinburgh's earliest surviving example of buildings grouped around an open court rather than a narrow close - restored in the 1960s with donations from benefactors including Harold Salvesen, it reopened as University of Edinburgh student housing in 1969 and remains so today.

name: Gladstone's Land
description: From the narrow Lawnmarket pavement, Gladstone's Land rises six full storeys above you, its ground-floor arcade recreating the timber shopfronts that once lined the whole Royal Mile before Victorian street-widening swept the rest away. The building beside you began around 1550, but it was the merchant Thomas Gledstanes and his wife Bessie Cunningham who rebuilt it from 1617, raising it to its present height and finishing by 1620 with the elaborately painted ceilings still visible inside. By the 1930s the Old Town had emptied out and the house faced demolition — the National Trust for Scotland saved it just in time, reopening it after a further £1.5 million refurbishment in 2021.
interesting_fact_1: A gilt-copper hawk hangs above the door — a pun on 'gled', old Scots for kite or hawk, playing on the Gledstanes name; inside, hunt the painted ceiling beams for a tiny hidden monkey among the 1620 decoration. The building's history has a darker side too: it reputedly once sold the era's supposed 'cures' for plague, and one resident, Lord Crichton, was scandalously rumoured to have started the fatal 1630 fire at Frendraught Castle to ruin a rival.

name: The Hub
description: Glance up at the corner of Castlehill and Johnston Terrace and you'll find Edinburgh's tallest spire, 71.7 metres of dark neo-Gothic stone piercing the skyline above you. Queen Victoria laid the foundation stone here in 1842 for Victoria Hall, a joint design by Scottish architect James Gillespie Graham and English Gothic Revival master Augustus Pugin, built to give the Church of Scotland's General Assembly a proper meeting place. It became Highland Tolbooth St John's Church in 1929, holding Gaelic and English services until closing in 1979 and standing empty for over a decade. A five-year, £7.5 million restoration — one of the most complex conservation projects ever undertaken in Scotland — reopened it in 1999 as The Hub, home of the Edinburgh International Festival.
interesting_fact_1: Pugin gave away the spire's design as a favour to his collaborator Graham — even though his own Roman Catholic church back in London, St George's, Southwark, never got a matching spire of its own. Despite its new life as a festival venue and cafe, the Church of Scotland's General Assembly still returns to meet inside every May, keeping alive the very purpose the hall was built for over 180 years ago.

name: Camera Obscura & World of Illusions
description: Inside, the top floor still does exactly what it did in 1853: a rotating mirror throws a live, moving image of the city outside onto a table in front of you — one of the oldest working camera obscuras in Britain. Getting here took a scandal: Maria Theresa Short arrived in Edinburgh in 1827 claiming to be the daughter of instrument-maker Thomas Short, who had died nearly 40 years before, a claim never proven but enough to win her his prized telescope. She opened an observatory on Calton Hill in 1835, was forced out by the council in 1849, and reopened here on Castlehill in 1853 as Short's Observatory. After her death, the pioneering planner Patrick Geddes took over in 1892, renaming it the Outlook Tower and stacking its floors with views of the world, Europe, Scotland and Edinburgh in ascending order beneath the camera obscura at the top.
interesting_fact_1: Category A listed since 1970, it's thought to be the oldest purpose-built visitor attraction in Edinburgh, with five further floors of the World of Illusions' mirror mazes and vortex tunnels since built beneath the original camera obscura. Geddes later built a second Outlook Tower in Montpellier, France, since absorbed into the Scots College there.

name: The Witchery by the Castle
description: Push through the door at Boswell's Court and candlelight closes around you — Gothic stone and low ceilings inside a merchant's townhouse raised in 1595 for Thomas Lowthian, later nicknamed for the eccentric physician Dr John Boswell, whose relatives James Boswell and Samuel Johnson once dined here. By the 1970s it had decayed into disused Church of Scotland committee rooms, until 20-year-old chef James Thomson bought it in 1979, becoming Scotland's youngest licensee at a time nobody rated the Royal Mile as restaurant territory. He expanded into the candlelit Secret Garden dining room in 1989, then into nine Gothic hotel suites, one entered through a hidden bookcase door. The name honours the hundreds burned as witches just up the street on Castlehill — locals still swear the building itself is haunted by one of them.
interesting_fact_1: A ghost-themed walking tour has met outside The Witchery every night since 1984, drawn by the same folklore that gives the restaurant its name.

name: The Scotch Whisky Experience
description: You're standing in a former Victorian school building right beside the Castle esplanade. For over three decades visitors rode through 300 years of whisky history inside mock oak barrels, past theatrical sets built by the team behind York's Jorvik Viking Centre, before a 2023 renovation retired the ride for three new galleries: Origins, The Art of Whisky Making and Maturation. The place exists because in 1988 whisky executive Alastair McIntosh persuaded nineteen Scotch companies to put up £2 million so visitors who couldn't reach the Highlands could still learn the spirit's history. Since 2009 it's also housed one man's obsession: 3,384 bottles gathered over 35 years by Brazilian collector Claive Vidiz, now a Guinness World Record holder for the largest Scotch whisky collection on Earth, its oldest bottle dating to 1897.
interesting_fact_1: Look for the chess set, the Scottie dog and the golf bags among Vidiz's bottles — whisky poured into some genuinely odd-shaped packaging over the decades. Downstairs, the Amber restaurant and bar stocks more than 420 single malts, blends and liqueurs; the attraction has welcomed more than 8.5 million visitors since 1988.

name: Tartan Weaving Mill
description: A viewing window over the basement workshop lets you watch a working heritage loom weave tartan cloth in real time — a rare working link to what this building actually was: Castlehill Reservoir, built in 1849-50 to supply the New Town with water. The huge cistern could hold two million gallons and empty it at 5,000 gallons a minute; workmen digging its foundations in 1851 turned up two oak log-coffins and a Roman coin of the Emperor Constantine, relics of the earlier Christ Church chapel demolished on this same spot to help build the Tron Kirk. Drained in 1992, it opened briefly for public tours the following year before being converted between 1995 and 1997 into what's now the Tartan Weaving Mill.
interesting_fact_1: Category B listed since 1987, the building still carries the Witches' Well fountain fixed to its outer wall, commemorating those burned nearby on Castlehill.

name: Cannonball House
description: The west-facing wall here still holds an iron cannonball still lodged in the stone — legend says it was fired from the Castle's Half Moon Battery at Bonnie Prince Charlie during the 1745 Jacobite rising. It's a better story than the truth: engineers most likely fixed it there around 1675 to mark the exact height gravity-fed water from springs at Comiston needed to reach before it could flow this far up the hill, Edinburgh's first piped water supply. The Category A listed house itself was built in 1630 for furrier Alexander Mure and his wife Margaret Niellems, their initials still carved above the door as 'AM MN 1630'. It later became a Castlehill School annexe in 1913, then an urban studies centre, before the Contini family turned it into a restaurant in 2014.
interesting_fact_1: The cannonball worked like a giant ballcock: when the water level in the reservoir below it dropped too far, it signalled that more needed to be pumped up from Comiston to keep the supply flowing.

name: Ramsay Garden
description: From below, Ramsay Garden's towers and white-harled walls seem to grow straight out of the castle rock — one of the most photographed skylines in Edinburgh, and one you can only admire from the street, since it's still private housing. It began in 1733 as an octagonal house built by the poet and wig-maker Allan Ramsay the Elder, its odd shape earning it the nickname 'the goose-pie house'. In 1890 the planner and biologist Patrick Geddes bought the site and rebuilt it as a deliberately mixed community of students, artisans and professionals, part of his campaign to drag Edinburgh's decaying Old Town back to life. Architect Stewart Henbest Capper designed the sixteen-apartment complex; Sydney Mitchell finished it after Capper's health failed. Geddes himself called the result 'the seven-towered castle I built for my beloved'.
interesting_fact_1: Past residents have included Ramsay's own descendants and the Royal Scottish Academy artist George Clark Stanton.

name: Castle Esplanade
description: This broad, flat expanse opens out to views north to the Firth of Forth and south to the Pentland Hills — free to take in without a Castle ticket. It was built in 1753 as a military parade ground, using spoil dug from the foundations of the Royal Exchange down on the High Street, then widened and given its present north wall and railings in 1816. Every August since 1950 it's been transformed into the site of the Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo — the first show had just eight items and drew 6,000 spectators to a single performance, compared with the roughly 10,000-seat temporary stadium built and dismantled here each summer today.
interesting_fact_1: Statues of Robert the Bruce and William Wallace flank the Castle's gatehouse at the esplanade's western end; scattered across its edges are a Witches' Well fountain, several regimental war memorials, and the grave of dragoon Charles Ewart, who captured a French standard at Waterloo in 1815.
