name: Edinburgh Castle
description: You're standing on the plug of an extinct volcano — Castle Rock has made this one of the most defensible sites in Scotland since at least the Iron Age, when a hillfort stood here some 3,000 years ago. It became a royal residence under King Malcolm III in the 11th century and was besieged more often than almost any fortress in Britain, including a night in 1314 when Thomas Randolph, Earl of Moray, led a party scaling the crag in darkness to recapture it from English hands. Today it holds the Honours of Scotland — the crown jewels — and the Stone of Destiny, used for centuries in Scottish coronations, though persistent rumour holds that the monks of Scone hid the real stone from Edward I and that what sits here is a substitute.
interesting_fact_1: St Margaret's Chapel inside the walls is the oldest surviving building in Edinburgh, built around 1130 by King David I for his canonised mother; barely large enough for a handful of people, it's still used for small weddings today. A gun still fires from Mills Mount Battery at 1pm each day (bar Sundays, Good Friday and Christmas) — a tradition begun in 1861 so ships on the Forth could set their chronometers when fog hid the time ball on Calton Hill's Nelson Monument.

name: The Witches' Well
description: Set into the wall at the foot of the esplanade, this small bronze relief marks Edinburgh's principal witch-burning ground, where an estimated 300 people were put to death on this spot alone. Patrick Geddes commissioned it in 1894 from his friend John Duncan, a leading figure of the Scottish Celtic Revival, fixing it to the wall of what was then the newly built Castlehill Reservoir. Look closely at the relief: a serene face and a wicked one, both entwined by a serpent coiled around Hygieia, Greek goddess of health, and her father Asclepius, god of medicine, with a sprig of foxglove worked in beside them — a heart medicine and a poison in one plant, a reminder that the same knowledge could heal or condemn whoever held it.
interesting_fact_1: Roman numerals worked into the bronze — 1479 and 1722 — bracket the two and a half centuries during which Scotland's Witchcraft Act was in force. Scotland executed an estimated 1,500 to 2,000 people for witchcraft between the 16th and 18th centuries, a persecution rate proportionally far higher than the more famous Salem trials three thousand miles away.

name: The India Cross
description: Trace the carving on this dark Celtic cross and among the entwined cable-work you'll find a stag's head and an elephant — the badge of the 78th Highlanders, raised here in 1862 to the 256 men of the regiment who died relieving the besieged garrison at Lucknow during the Indian Rebellion of 1857-58. Indian soldiers had risen against British rule that June; when the 78th fought through the rebel lines to reach the city that September, the whole regiment was voted the Victoria Cross by ballot, a mechanism reserved for acts of collective gallantry too widespread to credit to one man. The relieving commander, General Henry Havelock, is said to have declared he'd 'never seen better conduct — I am not a Highlander, but I wish I was one.'
interesting_fact_1: The elephant badge dates to the Battle of Assaye in 1803; decades later the 78th kept a real elephant as a regimental mascot at the Castle, and local legend has it that it drank the soldiers' beer at the canteen window. The 78th's lineage continues today within the Highlanders battalion of the Royal Regiment of Scotland.

name: Scottish Horse Memorial
description: This granite Celtic cross, carved with a claymore and a bronze lion rampant, was raised in 1904-05 to the Scottish Horse, a yeomanry regiment recruited from Scotland, Australia and South Africa in 1900 to fight Britain's brutal guerrilla campaign against Boer commandos in the Second Boer War. Look closely at the names and you'll find something unusual for a monument of this era: Zulu scouts who served and died alongside the regiment are named here too, a rare instance of Black South African soldiers being formally commemorated on a colonial-era war memorial. An identical cross stands on Caledonia Hill in Johannesburg, where it became the official war memorial of the Transvaal Scottish regiment. The Scottish Horse itself was disbanded at Edinburgh Castle in 1902; its lineage carries on today in the Scottish and North Irish Yeomanry.
interesting_fact_1: Sources disagree on exactly how many Zulu scouts are honoured — Edinburgh's own on-site panel says three, while accounts of the Johannesburg original say four.

name: The Afghan Needle
description: This pink Peterhead granite needle behind iron railings catches the wind coming straight off the esplanade, standing 3.5 metres tall and listed Grade II* by Historic Environment Scotland. Raised by public subscription in 1882-83, it commemorates the 105 officers, non-commissioned officers and men of the 72nd Duke of Albany's Own Highlanders who were killed in action or died of wounds and disease during the First and Second Anglo-Afghan Wars of 1839-42 and 1878-80. Read down its base and every name is grouped by how the man died — a stark ledger of two of the 19th century's bloodiest colonial campaigns, designed by the Aberdeen firm MacDonald, Field & Company. Locals simply call it the Afghan Needle.
interesting_fact_1: The 72nd amalgamated with the 78th Highlanders — commemorated by the India Cross a few steps away — to form the Seaforth Highlanders in 1881, only a year or two before this memorial went up; both regiments' lineage continues together today in the Highlanders battalion of the Royal Regiment of Scotland.

name: The Gatehouse
description: The drawbridge and the portcullis groove above the arch are still in full working order, but don't be fooled — the whole Gatehouse forming the Castle's grand entrance is Victorian, built in 1886-88 to give the fortress a more romantic approach befitting its status as a national monument. It was reportedly designed in some secrecy, since military authorities feared a cosmetic addition to a still-functioning garrison might draw public criticism. Flanking the archway in twin Gothic niches designed by architect Sir Robert Lorimer stand bronze statues of Robert the Bruce and William Wallace, added decades later in 1929 to mark the 600th anniversary of Bruce's death — a project so divisive it filled the Scottish press with argument throughout 1928 and 1929 before Thomas Clapperton and Alexander Carrick were finally chosen to sculpt the two figures.
interesting_fact_1: Funded by a bequest from Captain Hugh Reid, the statues were unveiled on 28 May 1929: Bruce, by Clapperton, wears his crown and carries an axe and shield; Wallace, by Carrick, grips a claymore.

name: Princess Louise's Fountain Memorial
description: The stone here is worn smooth and its bronze fittings have gone green with age, but look closely at the central panel and you can still make out a royal crown, a row of smaller crowns and an entwined monogram above twin drinking basins built into the esplanade wall. An inscription across the base names 'THE PRINCESS LOUISE'S ARGYLLSHIRE HIGHLANDERS' — a horse-trough and fountain erected in 1874 by the regiment, styled after their royal colonel-in-chief, Queen Victoria's daughter Princess Louise, Duchess of Argyll. The regiment itself took that name in 1881, when the 91st and 93rd Highlanders amalgamated. It's one of a cluster of regimental memorials dotted along the esplanade's edges.
interesting_fact_1: An identical horse-trough memorial to the same regiment stands on Stirling Castle's esplanade, the regiment's other historic depot. Princess Louise had a strong connection to Canada too — a province, a mountain range and several towns bear her name.

name: Robert the Bruce Statue
description: In the left-hand niche beside the Gatehouse stands Robert the Bruce in bronze, crowned and armoured, an axe in one hand and a heraldic shield in the other — sculptor Thomas J. Clapperton's pose recalling Bruce's single combat with the English knight Henry de Bohun on the eve of Bannockburn in 1314, when he split de Bohun's skull with one blow while mounted on nothing grander than a small palfrey. Unveiled on 28 May 1929, the 600th anniversary of Bruce's death, the statue only exists because a public design competition over how to portray Scotland's two great medieval heroes turned unexpectedly divisive, filling the Scottish press with argument through 1928 and 1929 before a compromise split the commissions between Clapperton and his rival sculptor.
interesting_fact_1: Bruce seized the Scottish throne in 1306, was excommunicated and hunted as a fugitive — the likely source of the probably apocryphal tale of a spider inspiring him to try again after defeat — before Bannockburn in 1314 secured Scotland's independence. He died in 1329 of an illness long assumed to be leprosy, though an 1819 examination of his skull found his missing teeth were more likely battle wounds; his heart was carried on crusade after his death and now lies at Melrose Abbey, while the rest of him is buried at Dunfermline Abbey.

name: William Wallace Statue
description: In the matching niche to the right of the archway stands William Wallace, sculpted by Alexander Carrick in chainmail and plaid, gripping a claymore with a helmet resting at his feet — unveiled the same day, 28 May 1929, as his Bruce counterpart opposite. Wallace led the rebel Scottish army to a stunning victory over a much larger English force at Stirling Bridge in 1297 and was appointed Guardian of Scotland, only to be defeated the following year at Falkirk. Betrayed and captured in 1305, he was dragged to London and executed as a traitor to a crown he'd never sworn allegiance to — a death that only hardened Scottish resistance and helped set up Bruce's victory at Bannockburn sixteen years later.
interesting_fact_1: Braveheart (1995) made Wallace world-famous but takes wide liberties with the history — the real Wallace almost certainly never wore a kilt, since the garment didn't yet exist in his lifetime.

name: Ensign Ewart Memorial and Grave
description: Beneath this granite memorial on the esplanade lies Charles Ewart, a Royal Scots Greys sergeant who fought off a standard-bearer, a lancer and an infantryman in quick succession at Waterloo in 1815 to capture the eagle standard of the French 45th Regiment — brutal hand-to-hand combat that made him a minor celebrity, promoted to Ensign and reportedly acquainted with Sir Walter Scott, though he claimed to shun the attention himself. He died in 1846 near Manchester and was buried in Salford, where the graveyard was later paved over and his grave forgotten. His remains were only rediscovered in the 1930s and reburied here with full military honours on 16 April 1938, nearly a century after his death.
interesting_fact_1: His own account of the fight survives almost word for word: 'I took the eagle from the enemy... he made a thrust at my groin; I parried it off and cut him down through the head.' In his memory, the Royal Scots Greys — and the Royal Scots Dragoon Guards that succeeded them — still wear an eagle badge today.

name: James' Court
description: Off the Lawnmarket, James' Court is a place where the noise falls away — a quiet close of 18th-century tenements behind Gladstone's Land, built from 1723-27 by James Brownhill and, for a while, one of Edinburgh's most fashionable addresses. The philosopher David Hume lived here before decamping to the grander New Town, and the diarist James Boswell later rented Hume's old flat. It was here in 1773 that Boswell hosted Samuel Johnson during the very trip through Scotland that produced Johnson's 'A Journey to the Western Islands of Scotland' — though the court Boswell knew burned down in 1857 and was rebuilt, so what stands around you now isn't quite the building the two men actually sat in.
interesting_fact_1: A plaque on one of the court's three arched entrances still commemorates the Hume-Boswell-Johnson connection.

name: The Jolly Judge

name: The Ensign Ewart

name: Johnston Terrace Wildlife Garden
description: Climb to the top of the Patrick Geddes Steps and you'll almost walk past this one - a scrap of green barely 50 metres from the Castle esplanade, squeezed between tenement walls. At just 0.07 hectares, it's the smallest of the Scottish Wildlife Trust's 123 Scottish nature reserves, but don't let the size fool you: listen for frogs and bumblebees, watch for grey herons overhead, and you're standing on ground that's cycled through more uses than almost anywhere else in the Old Town. A medieval chapel once stood here; later, Castlehill School children grew fruit and vegetables in it under town planner Patrick Geddes's influence, and it did a stretch of duty as a wartime military post before the Trust took it over in 1982 and turned it back into a patch of genuine urban wilderness.
interesting_fact_1: Before it became a nature reserve, generations of Castlehill School children spent their playtime growing fruit and vegetables here under Patrick Geddes's influence, and the plot also did a stint as a wartime military post - a resume most manicured gardens can't match. name: The Vennel and Flodden Wall
description: As you climb these worn stone steps, Edinburgh Castle appears to rise directly out of the rooftops ahead of you - it's one of the most photographed views in the city, and TV crews agree: both Ian Rankin's Rebus and the series One Day have filmed here. Partway up, run your hand along a genuine stretch of the Flodden Wall, thrown up in a hurry after Scotland's catastrophic 1513 defeat at Flodden left Edinburgh bracing for an English invasion. Near the top, where the wall gives way to the later Telfer Wall extension, you can still make out the crosslet gunloops of the surviving Flodden Tower bastion. The irony: the invasion everyone feared never actually arrived, so what you're touching is a monument to a siege that was prepared for at real expense and never came.

These days the steps do double duty as a working film set: the TV adaptation of Ian Rankin's Rebus used a door at the top of the Vennel as the detective's fictional home, and the series One Day filmed its own Edinburgh Castle shot from the same spot.

name: Tanner's Close, West Port
description: You're standing where the office block Argyle House now covers a site with a genuinely dark reputation: this was Tanner's Close, the lodging house where William Burke and William Hare ran an eleven-month, sixteen-victim killing spree in 1827-28 - Scotland's most notorious murder case. Rather than robbing graves like the "resurrectionists" of popular imagination, they smothered lodgers and drinking companions outright and sold the fresh bodies to Robert Knox, a prominent Edinburgh anatomist paying well and asking no questions. Hare only had a foothold here because he'd moved in with, then married, Margaret Logue, the widow of the close's previous keeper - meaning the murder floor was technically a family inheritance. Hare turned King's Evidence and walked free; Burke was hanged in 1828 before tens of thousands and was publicly dissected himself soon after.
interesting_fact_1: Burke's skeleton is still kept by the University of Edinburgh's Anatomical Museum, and a section of his skin was reportedly used to bind a small book, now held by Surgeons' Hall Museum - making him almost certainly the only Edinburgh murderer whose remains ended up on public display in two separate collections.

name: Beehive Inn
description: Duck under the Beehive's sign on the Grassmarket and you're standing in a building that's been taking in travellers since the 16th century, when mail coaches from the south would have stabled their horses right outside. Robert Burns reportedly stayed next door during his 1786-87 visits and watched cockfights held inside - a blood sport common in Scottish taverns of the day. Head up to the third-floor function room and you'll find the pub's oddest keepsake: the actual door of the death cell from Edinburgh's old Calton Jail. That same upstairs room is also where the Edinburgh Literary Pub Tour has kicked off every night since 1996, sending two actors and a crowd of visitors out to dramatise centuries of rivalry between Burns, Scott, Stevenson, Spark and the writers of Rebus and Harry Potter.

name: White Hart Inn
description: Parts of the building you're standing in front of date to 1516, making the White Hart a strong contender for the oldest continuously operating pub in central Edinburgh - and, by its own reckoning, the most haunted. Robert Burns stayed here in 1791, and William and Dorothy Wordsworth lodged here in 1803, but the guest list has a darker side too: Burke and Hare are said to have used the pub as a hunting ground for future victims among its regulars. Step outside and look down at the inscribed flagstone by the door - it marks where a bomb fell during a German Zeppelin raid on Edinburgh in April 1916, part of the earliest aerial attack the city ever endured. Staff and punters report more recent disturbances too: thrown bottles, pulled hair, and a figure seen in the cellar with no head.
interesting_fact_1: The Zeppelin raid of 2-3 April 1916 killed 13 people and injured two dozen more across Edinburgh that night - making the bomb that fell close to the White Hart Inn's door part of the earliest aerial attack the city ever endured, a strange piece of 20th-century wartime history layered onto a pub already three centuries old. Staff and regulars have reported hair being pulled, bottles thrown by unseen hands, and a headless figure glimpsed in the cellar - stories solid enough that the pub has marketed itself as Edinburgh's most haunted since 2005.

name: Petit Paris
description: Take a seat at one of Petit Paris's outdoor tables and you're looking straight up at Edinburgh Castle perched on its rock - one of the more dramatic backdrops for a plate of moules frites anywhere in the city. You're also sitting on ground with real history: the Grassmarket has been one of Edinburgh's main marketplaces since a royal charter in 1477, and for over a century from around 1660 it doubled as the city's execution site, where more than 100 Covenanters were hanged during the Killing Times. The restaurant itself opened in 1998 in a former branch of Pierre Victoire, the budget French bistro chain that collapsed that same year - founder Philippe Bachelet had cut his teeth working at Edinburgh's original Pierre Victoire since 1989, and his solo venture ended up outliving the very chain that trained him.

name: Patrick Geddes Steps

Geddes arrived in Edinburgh in 1884 and spent decades regenerating the Old Town's decaying tenements, most visibly a few steps up the hill at Ramsay Garden, which he redeveloped into flats between 1890 and 1893. The three doves stand for hand, heart and head - practical skill, feeling and thought - the trio Geddes believed any real work of civic improvement had to combine. At the top of these steps, a scrap of waste ground he once cleared survives today as the Johnston Terrace Wildlife Garden, still tended in his conservation-minded spirit.

name: Covenanters' Memorial
description: At your feet here, a cross of differently coloured cobblestones set into the pavement - laid out to mark the exact shadow once cast by Edinburgh's public gallows, which stood on this spot until the 1680s. More than 100 Covenanters, Presbyterians who refused to accept the crown's authority over the Church of Scotland, were hanged here between 1661 and 1688, most during the notorious 'Killing Time.' The gallows claimed ordinary criminals too - most famously Margaret 'Half-Hangit Maggie' Dickson, hanged in 1724 for concealing a pregnancy, who survived the drop and was found alive inside her coffin en route to burial. Because Scots law held her sentence already served, she had to legally remarry her own husband - and lived for decades more under her new nickname.

Because Scots law held that her sentence had already been carried out, the hanging had technically ended her marriage - so she had to legally remarry her own husband before resuming her life. A nearby pub still bears her name, marking the anniversary of her 'resurrection' with free beer.

name: Portsburgh Stone
description: A weathered, rounded boulder sits under a tree in the small walled garden off West Port - this is the Portsburgh Stone, and it's older than every building around you by tens of thousands of years. It's a glacial erratic, dragged here during the last Ice Age, possibly from the Corstorphine quarries across the city, though an older, more fanciful theory once claimed it was a fallen meteorite. It originally stood in Portsburgh, the burgh of barony that grew up here after 1649, before being built into a hostel's perimeter wall alongside two smaller companion stones. When that wall came down in 1905, the stone moved into the garden - and one of its two Ice-Age companions has since gone missing entirely somewhere in over a century of construction work nearby.

name: Hunter's Close
description: Walk into this narrow arched close at the Grassmarket's southeast corner and you're standing where a City Guard captain was lynched by his own city. In April 1736, after the hanging of smuggler Andrew Wilson turned into a riot, Captain John Porteous ordered his men to fire on the crowd, killing six. He was convicted of murder, but a royal reprieve from Queen Caroline delayed his execution - so on the night of 7 September 1736, a mob of thousands stormed the Tolbooth, dragged him out, and marched him here. He was hauled up this close and hanged from a dyer's pole with a rope taken from a nearby draper's shop, within sight of the gallows where he'd once commanded the firing squad. Sir Walter Scott used the episode as the opening set-piece of The Heart of Midlothian, and 'Porteous Mob' became shorthand for a city administering its own justice.

name: St Columba's by the Castle
description: Run your eye over the stonework of this Gothic church and you're looking at recycled royalty: much of it was quarried from the demolished palace of Mary of Guise, the 16th-century queen regent who ruled Scotland on behalf of her daughter, Mary, Queen of Scots, from 1554 until her death in 1560. The church itself went up in 1846-47 to designs by architect John Henderson, its layout shaped by the reforming ideas of the Oxford Movement within the Scottish Episcopal Church, and a day school beneath it once educated up to 200 local children. Look toward the east end and you'll find a striking mural of 'Christ Enthroned' by artist John Busby, installed in 1959 to fill a window that had sat blocked up for decades.

name: Fiddler's Arms
description: Settle in at the Fiddler's Arms and you're at the western end of a square that, right up until 1911, hosted Edinburgh's weekly horse and cattle market for close to 500 years - meaning this stretch of pavement was still ankle-deep in livestock trade barely a lifetime before today's regulars started ordering pints. The Old Town's wholesale trade once ran right past the pub's door too, through the neighbouring West Bow, where merchants dealt in iron, pitch, tar and hemp bound for warehouses down in Leith. True to its name, the pub still leans into a folk-music identity, with regular traditional Scottish sessions live every weekend - a nod to a Grassmarket long associated with market traders, drovers and travelling entertainers.

name: West Port Garden
description: Climb the terraced paths of this steep little garden and you're walking through a design nearly overlooked in the history books: West Port Garden was created in 1909 by town planner Patrick Geddes, but the actual layout - terraces carved into the slope between West Port and the College of Art - was the work of his daughter Norah, a professional landscape gardener in her own right at a time when few women held that title. It opened in June 1910 as one of several small green spaces Geddes carved into the crowded Old Town specifically so slum children could experience nature firsthand. Over a century later it's still community-run, now overseen by the Grassmarket Residents Association, hosting local people doing therapeutic gardening and growing their own food.

The square takes its name from the old Burgh of Portsburgh, an independent burgh that grew up outside Edinburgh's city walls near the West Port before being absorbed into the city in the 19th century - meaning the ground under your feet only became properly 'Edinburgh' relatively recently.

Despite the old-fashioned name, the steps underfoot are a modern addition, rebuilt in 2001 - and a stretch of the old Flodden Wall still runs alongside them, two very different pieces of Old Town history sharing the same stairwell.

description: This long, flat hollow beneath the Castle rock has been a marketplace since 1477, when a weekly market for hay, cattle and grain was first licensed here - a trade that carried on, remarkably, until 1911. But it's better known today for what happened at its east end: from 1660 until the last hanging in 1784, this was Edinburgh's public execution ground, watched by crowds that could number in the thousands.

Step inside and the walls themselves are built from 17th-century stone salvaged from the tenements that once crowded this square - the same stone that watched the drops fall. Order a pint here and you're drinking, quite literally, where condemned prisoners once had theirs.

Her coffin was carted off toward burial in Musselburgh, but when the driver stopped for lunch along the way, he found Maggie very much alive inside it. Scots law barred a second attempt at a sentence already carried out, so 'Half-Hangit Maggie' walked free - and, by local legend, went on to live for decades afterwards, eventually running a pub of her own on this same stretch of the Grassmarket.

name: George IV Bridge
description: From George IV Bridge, glancing down between the buildings, you'll catch just how high above the ground you really are - most of this street is a bridge in disguise. Architect Thomas Hamilton laid its foundation stone on 15 August 1827 to carry a new road from the Old Town's South Side over the Cowgate valley up to the Lawnmarket. Funding rows and disputes with the Edinburgh Improvement Commissioners dragged the build out for nearly a decade - Hamilton himself quit the project in 1834 - and the bridge wasn't finished until 1836. Underneath the shops, tenements and even a festival venue you're walking past sit nine semicircular stone arches; only two are still visible from outside.
interesting_fact_1: Building the bridge meant demolishing two historic streets outright, including Libberton's Wynd, which took with it John Dowie's Tavern - a tiny 18th-century howff where Robert Burns was a regular, favouring its smallest snug, nicknamed 'the coffin', which sat only four or six people at a squeeze.

name: National Library of Scotland
description: The grand stone facade of the National Library of Scotland fronts a project part-funded by biscuits. The library's roots go back to the Advocates Library, founded in the early 1680s, which won the right to a free copy of every book published in Britain under the Copyright Act of 1710. It only became a national institution in 1925, backed by a £100,000 endowment from Sir Alexander Grant - the man behind McVitie's biscuits - who later gave a further £100,000 toward this purpose-built home. Architect Reginald Fairlie's design began construction in the late 1930s, but wartime delays halted work for years; the building didn't fully open until 1956.
interesting_fact_1: By law the library is still entitled to a copy of virtually everything published in the UK and Ireland, in print or online - legal deposit has grown its holdings to somewhere around 30 million items, one of the largest research collections in Europe.

name: Edinburgh Central Library
description: Above the entrance of Edinburgh Central Library is Andrew Carnegie's personal motto carved into the stone: 'Let there be Light.' Carnegie insisted on those words above every library he funded, and this one only exists because he doubled his original £25,000 offer to £50,000 after being shown the site. Designed by George Washington Browne in an ornate French Renaissance style, the building actually drops away below street level, with further storeys descending through the gorge toward the Cowgate. Look for the carved stone lintel built into the wall, inscribed 'TECUM HABITA 1616' - salvaged from Sir Thomas Hope's townhouse, which stood on this spot three centuries before the library did.
interesting_fact_1: Carnegie wasn't even present when Lord Rosebery officially opened the building on 9 June 1890 - a telegram from Carnegie was read out instead, hoping 'that this Library is to grow in usefulness year after year.' Edinburgh is still the only local authority in the UK that classifies its adult library collection using the Library of Congress system rather than Dewey Decimal.

name: Victoria Street
description: Victoria Street's single curling bow of rainbow shopfronts is one of the most photographed streets in Scotland - though it started life as something much uglier. This was the West Bow, a notoriously crooked, dangerous medieval route linking the Grassmarket to the Royal Mile, until architect Thomas Hamilton swept much of it away between 1827 and 1834 as part of Edinburgh's Improvement Act works. Renamed in 1837 to mark Queen Victoria's accession, the street's two-tier design left an upper walkway, Victoria Terrace, running along its northern side above the shops you're browsing now.
interesting_fact_1: Its older name carries darker history: in 1670 the respected soldier Major Thomas Weir confessed on his deathbed to decades of black magic, incest and worse, and was burned at the stake as the self-styled 'Wizard of the West Bow'. Centuries later the street is widely credited, if unofficially, as an inspiration for Diagon Alley - J.K. Rowling worked for years at the Elephant House on George IV Bridge, a few minutes' walk from its top end, and would have passed this way often.

name: The Red Door Gallery
description: Spot the scarlet doorway at number 42 and you've found one of the shopfronts most responsible for Victoria Street's rainbow reputation: the Red Door Gallery. Inside, contemporary screenprints and giclee art prints share shelf space with designer jewellery, enamel pins, knitwear and handmade greetings cards from around 150 UK and Scottish artists - independent, small-run work rather than mass-produced tourist stock. It's one of dozens of small, owner-run shops that have filled Victoria Street's curved Georgian frontages since the street's 1830s construction, keeping independent retail alive on one of the most photographed streets in the country.
interesting_fact_1: The gallery is open all seven days of the week, year-round - a rarity among small independent Old Town shops, and a sign of just how much passing footfall Victoria Street's photogenic curve now draws.

name: Victoria Terrace
description: Climb the narrow flight of steps just off Victoria Street and you'll come out onto Victoria Terrace, an iron-railed balcony walkway laid along the rooftops of the shops below. Lean on the railing and the view runs straight down over Victoria Street's curved, candy-coloured shopfronts to the Grassmarket, and up the other way to Edinburgh Castle on its rock. This is the surviving upper deck of Thomas Hamilton's 1827-34 rebuilding of the old West Bow - the same trick he pulled off a few streets over with George IV Bridge: a street built up on hidden lower levels, so what looks like solid ground beneath your feet is really a bridge or terrace over the buildings and streets below.
interesting_fact_1: It's one of the few places in the Old Town where you can look straight down onto a whole street from a walkway built directly above its shops.

name: The Oz Bar
description: Push through the ramshackle tin awning on Candlemaker Row and you'll trade Old Town stone for corrugated iron and outback-shed kitsch: the Oz Bar has given Edinburgh's Australian community and expats a home-away-from-home since 1997. name: West Bow Well
description: The carved stone wellhead at the foot of Victoria Street is Edinburgh's very first public wellhead, erected in 1674 by master mason Robert Mylne. Water carried down from reservoirs fed by springs in the Pentland Hills arrived here first, and this became the start of the line for the city's water caddies - workers who queued at this exact spot to fill their kegs before hauling water door to door through the tenements above the Grassmarket. A semi-circular drinking basin sits below a 19th-century Edinburgh coat of arms on one face, with a smaller ornamental basin and heraldic panel on the others.
interesting_fact_1: A small iron door on the well still carries its original inscription: 'The West-Bow Well erected by the Town Council 1674. Repaired & altered by Richardson Brothers, merchants, West Bow, 1861.' Above the coat of arms runs the Latin motto 'Nisi Dominus Frustra' - 'without God, everything fails' - the same words that still appear on Edinburgh's own civic coat of arms today.

name: Museum Context
description: Museum Context on Victoria Street holds two histories stacked on top of each other. For more than 130 years, from 1873 until 2004, this building housed Robert Cresser's brush shop, a Victorian ironmonger-style store crammed with brooms and brushes hanging from the ceiling and stuffed onto shelves, so cluttered and Dickensian that people travelled from across the UK just to see it. Today it's one of the city's best-known officially licensed Harry Potter shops, three floors of wands, house scarves and robes - but the original Victorian wooden fittings survive largely intact behind the modern merchandise, giving the warren of small rooms an uncannily Ollivanders-like feel that long predates any Potter theme.
interesting_fact_1: The top floor has a free photo spot with props and house robes, including a mirror etched with the 'Chamber of Secrets' inscription - playing up the wider theory that this curving street, a short walk from where J.K. Rowling wrote much of the early books, inspired Diagon Alley itself.

name: The Enchanted Galaxy
description: The shop at the top of Victoria Street didn't get its name easily. Run by the Gold brothers, it originally opened as 'The Boy Wizard' - a name Warner Bros. objected to as trading too directly on Harry Potter trademarks, pursuing the dispute through the High Court. name: John Kay's Shop
description: The small green-fronted shop at the top of Victoria Street sells prints, postcards and Scottish mementos, and takes its name from a barber who gave up cutting hair to draw. John Kay (1742-1826) worked as an Old Town barber until his sketching hobby overtook his trade; by 1785 he had opened a print shop of his own in Parliament Close, producing etched caricatures of the city's great and ordinary figures alike. Over almost 900 plates between 1784 and 1822, he documented everyone from Enlightenment intellectuals to street vendors, most sketched from nothing more than a passing glance - leaving one of the richest visual records of Georgian Edinburgh life.
interesting_fact_1: The modern shop is a separate business, incorporated in 2017, rather than a surviving continuation of Kay's own print shop, which stood roughly half a mile away in Parliament Close - but its stock of prints, maps and Scottish curiosities makes the name a fitting tribute rather than a coincidence.

name: India Buildings
address: India Buildings, Victoria Street, Edinburgh EH1 2EX
description: Inside India Buildings, a domed rotunda ringed by balconies opens overhead inside what looks, from the curved street outside, like just another four-storey Scots Baronial office block. Built between 1864 and 1866 to designs by architect David Cousin, its name was likely borrowed from a Liverpool office block of the 1830s, itself named by merchants celebrating the end of the East India Company's monopoly on trade with India. It originally housed serious institutional tenants, including the British Linen Bank, projecting financial weight onto a street otherwise defined by small shops and closes.

name: Augustine United Church
description: The tiered, ornamental tower on George IV Bridge explains its long-running nickname: the 'bride's-cake' tower, so called for its layered, iced-looking profile. Augustine United Church's congregation traces back to 1802, when Reverend John Aikman founded a church nearby - on what's now the site of the National Museum of Scotland - out of Edinburgh's radical Reformation tradition. The current building, put up between 1857 and 1861 by architects J J & W H Hay, blends Romanesque, Renaissance and Classical detailing, its restored tower still the street's most distinctive silhouette.
interesting_fact_1: The congregation's roots lie in one of Edinburgh's most deprived districts, where working families and their livestock once lived crowded beneath the wealthy merchants and academics of the Royal Mile above - a history the church still cites as the root of its long-running social and community engagement.

name: Frankenstein & Bier Keller

name: Edinburgh Sheriff Court
description: The ornate iron gateway and postbox-style enquiry point at the entrance are a small formal touch from an era when court buildings were built to visibly project authority to everyone passing on the street. Sheriff court business in Edinburgh has moved through several homes over the centuries: an 1816 county hall on the corner of Lawnmarket and George IV Bridge, then a purpose-built Renaissance Revival courthouse designed by David Bryce and completed in 1868, before hearings eventually relocated to this Chambers Street building. The office of procurator fiscal that prosecutes cases through this court traces back even further, with the earliest documented references in Scottish records dating to the 1550s.
interesting_fact_1: The Sheriff Court and the adjoining Justice of the Peace Court still share that same gateway - a small architectural detail linking two branches of Scottish justice that both trace back centuries before either building existed.

name: Crown Office
description: The Crown Office's imposing 268-foot Renaissance facade on Chambers Street, borrowing details from a French chateau, belongs to a building that started life as a college, not a prosecutor's office. Built from 1872-74 to designs by David Rhind (with David Cousin and John Lessels), it was originally the Watt Institution and School of Arts, which in 1885 merged with the centuries-old George Heriot's Trust to become Heriot-Watt College - the direct ancestor of today's Heriot-Watt University. The facade was designed to give a technical college the civic gravity of a bank or courthouse, gravity the building has kept ever since, just in service of a different institution: the headquarters of the body that investigates and prosecutes crime across all of Scotland.
interesting_fact_1: Heriot-Watt University's own roots run through this one Chambers Street address before the college eventually outgrew it and moved to its present Riccarton campus - meaning Scotland's chief prosecuting authority now works out of what was, in effect, an early ancestor of a modern Scottish university.

name: Victoria Street's Cobbles
description: At your feet on Victoria Street are setts, not cobbles - roughly cut rectangular granite blocks bedded into sand and gravel, a paving technique once universal across the Old Town. Streets were paved this way from the 18th century onward because granite setts were durable enough to survive horse-drawn cart traffic and could be re-laid individually when damaged, unlike a continuous surface. Most of Edinburgh's other streets have long since been resurfaced in tarmac for modern traffic, making this curving run of setts - visibly worn smooth by two centuries of footfall and cartwheels - one of the best-preserved and most photographed stretches of historic paving left in the city.
interesting_fact_1: The double yellow lines painted directly onto the historic setts are a small, constant tension point for conservation bodies - modern traffic regulation applied directly on top of 19th-century stonework, on a street that's otherwise treated as one of Edinburgh's most protected historic assets.

name: Quaker Meeting House
address: 7 Victoria Terrace, above, Victoria St, Edinburgh EH1 2JL, UK
description: This Italian Gothic building on Victoria Terrace has changed hands, and purposes, more than once. Built in 1865-66 as a chapel for the United Original Secession Church, it was sold in 1956 to the Boys' Brigade, who had it remodelled by Basil Spence Architects and used it as their Edinburgh Battalion headquarters, known as Kirk House. The Religious Society of Friends converted it into Edinburgh's Quaker Meeting House in 1987, finally giving the city's Quaker community - which had first formed a small central Edinburgh meeting back in 1924 - a permanent, fully accessible home.
interesting_fact_1: Before settling here, Edinburgh's Central Meeting spent almost fifty years, from 1938 to 1987, gathering in a building on Stafford Street in the New Town.

name: Chambers Street
description: This whole street didn't exist before 1871 - it was cut straight through a warren of slum housing under the Edinburgh Improvement Act of 1867, the same clearance that swept away three entire 18th-century squares nearby. It's named after the man who pushed the Act through: publisher and Lord Provost William Chambers, of the Chambers's dictionary and encyclopaedia firm, who used his position to remake this whole corner of the Old Town around a single grand purpose - housing Scotland's national museum.
interesting_fact_1: The museum's foundation stone was laid on 23 October 1861, in a ceremony that turned out to be Prince Albert's very last public appearance - he died less than two months later, making this one of the final things he ever did in public life.
interesting_fact_2: William Chambers rose from a small bookshop in Peebles to build one of the 19th century's biggest reference-book publishing empires with his brother Robert, and poured his fortune and his final years as Lord Provost into rebuilding this district. He died in 1883, the same decade his namesake street's grand museum buildings were finally completed.

name: Greyfriars Hall
description: Passing along the Cowgate, a Gothic tower with pointed windows breaks the skyline where you'd expect an ordinary tenement front - that's Greyfriars Hall, once Cowgatehead Church. Built around 1861 for one of Edinburgh's crowded Old Town parishes, the church eventually lost its congregation and stood empty for years, until Virgin Hotels Edinburgh restored it in 2022, stitching it together with two neighbouring historic buildings to form the hotel. Walk around the tower and you'll see a glass-fronted extension bolted onto the old stone, housing the hotel's modern guest floors, while inside, the original nave's vaulted ceiling and stone tracery survive intact, now used as an event space seating up to 150.
interesting_fact_1: The trio of linked buildings is anchored by the Category A-listed India Buildings on Victoria Street, built in 1864 - the church itself, listed Category B, is the junior partner architecturally even though it's the most eye-catching from the Cowgate. ICA Studio's Susannah Macneill first sketched the plan to link the old church with its neighbours back in 2013 - meaning the glass-and-stone building visible today took the better part of a decade to go from that first drawing to a finished hotel.

name: Tomb of John Bayne of Pitcairlie
description: A carved hand on this weathered mausoleum, built into Greyfriars' boundary wall, clutches a small purse - a nod to the royal signet, emblem of the man buried inside. John Bayne of Pitcairlie was a writer to the signet who made his fortune supervising the building contracts for Charles II's 1670s renovation of Holyrood Palace, working alongside architects Sir William Bruce and Robert Mylne on major Edinburgh projects including Canongate Kirk and the Tron Kirk. When he died in 1681, his widow Eupham Aikman won the Town Council's permission to raise this monument; masons Philip Alisone and Patrick Hunter built it, and James Andersone painted and gilded the carved surface, which still carries its long Latin inscription.
interesting_fact_1: That carved purse holding the royal signet is a direct nod to Bayne's own career - and beyond the mausoleum, he's also remembered for funding student bursaries at the universities of St Andrews and Edinburgh, a philanthropic streak that outlasted his legal work.

name: Greyfriars Kirk
description: At the edge of its own kirkyard just off George IV Bridge is Edinburgh's first church built after the Reformation - Greyfriars Kirk, which opened on Christmas Day 1620 on land that had belonged to a Franciscan friary until Reformers destroyed it in 1559. Look closely at the plain harled walls and squat tower: a gunpowder magazine stored inside that tower by the Town Council exploded in 1718, wrecking two-thirds of the structure and forcing a rebuild that split the church into two separate congregations, Old and New Greyfriars, worshipping side by side until they reunited in 1929. It remains an active Church of Scotland parish today, its modest exterior giving little hint of the momentous scene that played out just outside its door in 1638.
interesting_fact_1: The National Covenant - a mass declaration against royal interference in Scottish worship - was laid out on a flat tombstone in the churchyard on 28 February 1638 for signing, and within weeks copies had circulated the country so widely that tens of thousands of Scots had added their names, some reputedly signing in their own blood.

name: Greyfriars Kirkyard
description: Walk between the crowded rows of table tombs and grand mausolea and you're standing in one of Edinburgh's oldest burial grounds - Greyfriars Kirkyard, granted to the town by Mary Queen of Scots in 1562 on land that had belonged to a Franciscan friary, the 'grey friars' whose robes gave the site its name. With the Old Town's older kirkyards long full, generations of merchants, lawyers and reformers came to rest here, leaving one of the richest collections of post-Reformation funerary architecture in Scotland. Somewhere among the unmarked ground lies James Craig, the young architect who won the competition to design Edinburgh's New Town but died in poverty. Just inside the main gate on Candlemaker Row, a small headstone marks where Bobby, the loyal terrier whose statue stands at this leg's end, was buried in 1872.
interesting_fact_1: By the early 1800s the kirkyard was so tempting a target for body-snatchers supplying the city's anatomy schools that grieving families began fitting heavy iron cages called mortsafes over freshly dug graves - several 'double-bedder' mortsafes from the late 1820s can still be seen bolted in place near the boundary walls today.

name: Covenanters' Prison
address: Greyfriars Kirkyard (Forrest Road side), Edinburgh EH1 2QL
description: Peer through the locked iron gate off Candlemaker Row into the walled enclosure known as the Covenanters' Prison and you're looking at open ground with a brutal history. After the Covenanter army was crushed at the Battle of Bothwell Bridge in June 1679, around 1,200 prisoners were marched here and held in the open air for more than four months, each allotted just four ounces of bread a day; dozens died of exposure and starvation before winter set in, while others were tried and executed or escaped. In November 1679, some 257 survivors sentenced to transportation to the American colonies were marched to Leith and put aboard the Crown of London - it wrecked off Orkney soon after, and the crew battened the hatches shut, drowning over 200 men still shackled below deck.
interesting_fact_1: The grand mausolea now crowded inside the enclosure mostly date from after 1705, when the ground was formally laid out for burials - meaning almost none of the monuments a visitor sees today existed when the Covenanters were actually confined here in the open air in 1679.

name: The Black Mausoleum
description: A domed, colonnaded tomb tucked against Greyfriars' southern boundary wall is the Black Mausoleum, built for Sir George Mackenzie of Rosehaugh - the King's Advocate who prosecuted the Covenanters imprisoned just metres away and earned the nickname 'Bloody Mackenzie' for the executions he ordered during the Killing Time. Designed by architect James Smith and completed shortly before Mackenzie's death in 1691, its drum-shaped form was unusual for Restoration-era Scotland. Mackenzie was also a founding force behind the Advocates' Library, later absorbed into the National Library of Scotland just up the street - a rather more respectable legacy than the one that's made this tomb one of the most 'haunted' sites in Britain.
interesting_fact_1: In 1998 a homeless man sheltering inside broke through an iron floor grating and fell into an underground vault, crashing through a 17th-century coffin lid into a mass of bones and dust - an incident locals blame for waking the so-called 'Mackenzie Poltergeist', whose reported scratches, bruises and faintings led the kirkyard's keyholder to have the tomb locked and exorcised in 1999. Tour guides and fan sites sometimes link the legend to Peeves, Hogwarts' resident poltergeist in the Harry Potter books, though J.K. Rowling has never confirmed any connection between the two.

name: Greyfriars Bobby's Bar
description: This bar at the foot of Candlemaker Row occupies a Category B listed pub occupying the ground floor of early Georgian houses built as part of the same 1720s development as the neighbouring Candlemakers' Hall. Long a tavern under other names, it was renamed Greyfriars Bobby's Bar after the small terrier whose statue - cast by sculptor William Brodie and unveiled in 1873, a year after the dog's death - stands on the pavement just outside its door. Inside, dark wood panelling and old photographs of the real Bobby lean into the legend, while the pub's position squarely between the kirkyard gate and the statue makes it one of the most photographed backdrops on this stretch of the walk.
interesting_fact_1: Rub Bobby's nose outside and you're adding to decades of wear that has stripped away the statue's black patina to a bright bronze shine - Edinburgh City Council has had the bronze professionally re-blackened more than once, only for the statue to be vandalised again within days of one 2013 restoration.

name: Bedlam Theatre
description: At the corner of Forrest Road and Bristo Place stands a red sandstone Gothic front with a steep gabled roof and lancet windows - built in 1848 for the New North Free Church by Thomas Hamilton, one of the architects behind the Scott Monument and the Royal High School. The congregation left in 1941, and after decades serving as a University of Edinburgh chaplaincy and storeroom, students converted the deconsecrated church into a theatre in 1980-81, keeping the Gothic shell intact. Step inside today and you're in the oldest continuously running student theatre in Britain, staging around forty University of Edinburgh Theatre Company productions a year and packing in up to eight separate Fringe shows a day every August.
interesting_fact_1: The theatre takes its name not from the church but from the area's earlier history: this stretch of Forrest Road once stood beside Edinburgh's 'Bedlam', a poorhouse and asylum, where the poet Robert Fergusson - a major influence on the young Robert Burns - died in 1774 at just twenty-four.

name: Greyfriars Bobby Statue
address: Corner of George IV Bridge & Candlemaker Row, Edinburgh EH1 2QQ
description: At the corner of George IV Bridge and Candlemaker Row, opposite the kirkyard gate, stands what's said to be the smallest listed structure in Edinburgh - a life-size bronze statue and drinking fountain standing barely a foot tall. Sculpted by William Brodie and unveiled in November 1873, it was funded by the English philanthropist Baroness Angela Burdett-Coutts, whose name is still cast into the bronze plaque on its granite base. It commemorates a small terrier who, according to Edinburgh legend, kept vigil for fourteen years at the grave of his master, night watchman John Gray, just across the road.
interesting_fact_1: Edinburgh's Lord Provost, Sir William Chambers, was taken enough with the story that in 1867 he personally paid for the dog's licence and had him fitted with a collar, now on display in the Museum of Edinburgh. Yet Bobby's story is one of the most disputed in Edinburgh folklore: historian Jan Bondeson has traced more than sixty similar 'faithful graveyard dog' tales recorded across 19th-century Europe, and argues the original dog was probably a stray fed by sympathetic visitors, with a different, younger dog likely taking over the vigil after the first one died.

name: Greyfriars Bobby's Grave
address: Greyfriars Kirkyard, Edinburgh EH1 2QQ (just inside the main gate)
description: Just inside Greyfriars Kirkyard's main gate, near the George IV Bridge entrance, is a small red granite headstone marking the traditional burial spot of Greyfriars Bobby. The stone is much newer than the 1872 burial it commemorates - it was erected by the Dog Aid Society of Scotland and unveiled by the Duke of Gloucester on 13 May 1981, more than a century after Bobby's death. His actual grave lies some seventy-five yards from his master John Gray's, since dogs couldn't normally be buried inside the kirkyard - a small, unofficial exception made for the city's most famous mourner. Look down at the foot of the stone and you'll usually find sticks, dog toys and collars left by visitors rather than flowers.

Watching ordinary erosion and sediment deposition at work in the Scottish landscape around him, Hutton argued that the same slow forces, acting over immense stretches of time, had shaped the entire Earth - a theory of 'deep time' that upended the far shorter Biblical timelines then generally assumed. He presented his Theory of the Earth to the Royal Society of Edinburgh in 1785 and published an expanded edition a decade later.

name: William Chambers Monument
description: This statue on the widened plaza outside the National Museum of Scotland honours Sir William Chambers (1800-1883), the publisher-turned-Lord-Provost who reshaped this part of the Old Town more than almost anyone else. He and his brother Robert built a printing and publishing empire from a small Peebles bookshop, but it was as Lord Provost from 1865 that Chambers left his biggest mark, pushing through the 1867 Edinburgh Improvement Act, which cleared entire slum closes and cut new streets - including the one that now bears his name - through some of the city's most overcrowded ground. Sculpted by John Rhind, the statue went up in 1891, originally standing in the middle of Chambers Street itself.

name: Cowgate
description: Everything about the Cowgate sits below the Royal Mile in more than one sense - literally lower down the valley, and for most of its history, socially lower too. Its name is exactly what it sounds like: this was once 'Via Vaccarum', the route drovers used to bring cattle down from the fields south and east of the city to the market at the Grassmarket, back when driving livestock through the main streets above was against the law.
interesting_fact_1: The Cowgate wasn't always poor - Cardinal David Beaton, one of the most powerful churchmen in 16th-century Scotland, kept a residence here so grand that contemporaries called it a palace. By the 19th century the same street had become one of Edinburgh's worst slums, its fortunes falling as the wealthy retreated to the New Town.
interesting_fact_2: When South Bridge was built high overhead in the 1780s, the space beneath its arches - entered at Cowgate level - was built out into vaults, first used for storage and workshops, then, as conditions worsened through the 19th century, into some of the most squalid housing anywhere in the city. Those same vaults are now Edinburgh's best-known ghost-tour attraction.
interesting_fact_3: Today the Cowgate runs in the opposite direction from its history: during the Edinburgh Festival Fringe every August, this stretch becomes one of the most densely packed nightlife strips in Scotland, its old workshops and stables now bars and clubs.

name: Sandy Bell's
description: Push through the door and the first thing that hits you is the fiddle — a tune sawing away in the corner, glasses keeping time, the smell of hops and old wood. This unassuming corner pub has been Edinburgh's living room for traditional music since 1942. It started life as the Forrest Hill Buffet, then the Forrest Hill Bar, before taking the name of Mrs Bell, who ran it in the 1920s — nobody now remembers who "Sandy" was. Its real fame came during the Scottish Folk Revival of the 1950s–70s, when it became the movement's unofficial headquarters. Folklorist Hamish Henderson drank here for decades; his bust still watches the bar. In the 1970s, a live album, Sandy Bell's Ceilidh, was recorded on the premises with Aly Bain and Dick Gaughan among the players.
interesting_fact_1: There have been traditional music sessions at Sandy Bell's continuously since 1942, and in the 1970s the pub's live scene was captured on the album Sandy Bell's Ceilidh, featuring Aly Bain and Dick Gaughan. A bust of folklorist Hamish Henderson, a regular until his death in 2002, still hangs above the bar.

name: Bristo Port (Flodden Wall)
address: Forrest Road (between nos. 5 and 7), Edinburgh EH1 2QQ
description: Between numbers 5 and 7 Forrest Road is something odd: a narrow gap in the tenement line, filled in at the bottom, that doesn't quite match its neighbours. That seam is where Edinburgh's city wall once stood. After the catastrophic defeat at Flodden in 1513, a panicked city rushed to enclose itself, throwing up what's now called the Flodden Wall. A fortified gateway, Bristo Port, once stood near here, letting traffic through the defences before it was demolished around 1715 once the wall had outlived its purpose. Walk a little further along and you'll find another stretch of the same wall reused as the outer face of a tenement, its old stonework simply pierced for windows.
interesting_fact_1: The Flodden Wall was built in a rush after Scotland's disastrous 1513 defeat at the Battle of Flodden, and Bristo Port, the fortified gateway that once stood here, was likely demolished around 1715 once the wall was no longer needed.

name: Teviot Row House
description: Notice how the students treat this building like it's theirs — because, in a very real sense, it was the first place in the world where that was true. Opened on 19 October 1889, Teviot Row House is the oldest purpose-built student union building on Earth, designed by Sydney Mitchell and Wilson and extended twice since. It grew out of the Students' Representative Council's 1884 campaign for a proper home of their own. For most of its history it was a men-only stronghold — women weren't admitted as members until a vote finally passed on 5 January 1971, requiring a 75% majority. It took until 1972 for every matriculated student to become an automatic member, closing out a century of exclusivity.
interesting_fact_1: Teviot Row House, opened in 1889, is believed to be the oldest purpose-built student union building in the world - though women weren't admitted as members until a vote passed on 5 January 1971, which needed a 75% majority to succeed.

name: Reid Concert Hall
description: In front of its solid Victorian columns, imagine rows of glass cases holding sackbuts, serpents and clarinets instead of lecture-goers — because for well over a century, this building held one of the strangest collections in Edinburgh. Opened in 1859 as the Reid School of Music, it became home to what's believed to be the world's earliest museum of musical instruments, eventually growing to display around a thousand pieces spanning 400 years, including the celebrated Sir Nicholas Shackleton clarinet collection. In 2017, following a major restoration of St Cecilia's Hall, the entire collection was quietly moved across town, leaving this grand hall to carry on its academic life without the instruments that made it famous.
interesting_fact_1: The Reid Concert Hall housed what is believed to be the world's earliest museum of musical instruments, until the collection was relocated to St Cecilia's Hall in 2017 after a £6.5 million restoration there.

name: McEwan Lantern Pillar
description: Cross the square and you'll spot it standing alone — an ornate stone pillar topped with a lantern, looking almost too decorative for a public square, its surface carved with a coat of arms you might not recognise. That crest belongs to William McEwan, the Edinburgh brewing magnate whose beer money built the flamboyant McEwan Hall facing you across the square. Erected in 1897 to mark the Hall's opening on 3 December that year, the pillar was McEwan's personal gift to the city, a quieter companion piece to his more famous, much grander donation. Between them, the pillar and the Hall form a kind of one-man monument to Victorian Edinburgh's love affair with beer money and civic generosity.
interesting_fact_1: The pillar was a personal gift to the city from brewing magnate William McEwan, who also funded McEwan Hall, and was erected in 1897 to mark the hall's opening on 3 December that year.

It's easy to walk straight over them without noticing — which is rather the point. This is a public artwork by artist Susan Collis, made up of roughly 1,600 bronze dots set into the stone, tracing a path from near the Dugald Stewart Building all the way to the grand entrance of McEwan Hall. Unlike the square's imposing Victorian architecture, it asks for nothing — no plinth, no plaque demanding attention — just a quiet trail of little things you're free to discover for yourself.

name: The Gilded Saloon
description: The gold lettering above the door catches the light before anything else does, and if you listen you might catch a burst of laughter or a snatch of music drifting up from below street level — this place has performance in its bones. The original Gilded Saloon opened in the Cowgate, a beloved haunt for local comics, poets and musicians, until it was destroyed in the devastating 2002 Cowgate fire that also took eleven neighbouring businesses with it. It took over two decades for the name to return, when Gilded Balloon joined forces with Paradise Palms and Kelburn Arts to open this new venue on Lothian Street just before the 2025 Fringe, complete with a 200-capacity performance space downstairs.

name: Old Medical School
description: Run your eye along the honey-coloured stone of this sprawling Renaissance-style facade and picture the generations of medical students who passed beneath it clutching bags of surgical instruments. For 118 years, until the school moved out to Little France in 2002, this was the beating heart of Edinburgh's medical training, an institution once considered the finest in the English-speaking world. Designed by Sir Rowand Anderson and built between 1876 and 1886, it's forever tied to Joseph Lister, who returned to Edinburgh as Professor of Surgery in 1869 and, working nearby, pioneered the antiseptic techniques that made modern surgery survivable. name: George Heriot's School (Main Building)
description: Golden sandstone, a vast quadrangle, turrets catching the light at every corner — it's easy to see why this place stops people in their tracks. The building's existence traces back to one man's guilty conscience, or perhaps his ambition: George Heriot, royal goldsmith and moneylender to James VI, earned the nickname "Jinglin' Geordie" from the coins rattling in his pockets as he made his rounds of the city. In 1621 he arranged for his fortune to found a hospital and school for fatherless children, though he didn't live to see it — the building was completed and opened as George Heriot's Hospital in 1659. Its imposing Lauriston Place archway, added later by architect William Henry Playfair, remains the grand public face of the school today.

description: Feel the avenue open up around you — a broad, tree-lined path running dead straight across open parkland, the kind of quiet green corridor that feels like it shouldn't exist this close to a city centre. It very nearly didn't survive. Laid out by Thomas Hope after 1722 as a raised causeway across a drained loch, over 1,200 trees were later planted along its length, and by 1850 it was marked at either end by ornamental pillars topped with stone unicorns. Since then it has repelled one threat after another: Victorian planners wanted it widened for carriages, and as late as the 1960s the city seriously considered driving a six-lane motorway straight through the Meadows.

name: Doctors

Built in 1874 to mark the opening of the old Royal Infirmary across the road, it originally housed small trades that fed off the hospital's business: a cabinet-and-coffin maker traded here from 1884 to 1959, and a maker of surgical instruments carried on into the early 1960s. Only after those tenants left did it become a bar, first a short-lived barbecue joint, then a pub called The Mortar from 1970, before finally settling on its current, fitting name, Doctors, in 1979.

name: Edinburgh Futures Institute
description: Take in the turreted, sandstone bulk in front of you — it looks far more like a Scottish castle than a university building, and that's because it was built to heal, not to teach. Completed in 1879 to designs by architect David Bryce, this was the old Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh, its ward pavilions deliberately spaced apart in the fresh air beside the Meadows to reduce the spread of infection, cutting-edge thinking for its time. The hospital served the city until 2003, when it relocated south to Little France. The University bought the site in 2016 and spent seven years and millions of pounds restoring it, reopening the building to the public in June 2024 as a hub for interdisciplinary research, with new public gardens and walkways carved through the old infirmary grounds.

name: Simpson Loan
description: A quiet residential street of glass and stone now, but the name overhead nods to one of medicine's more reckless breakthroughs. James Young Simpson, an Edinburgh professor of midwifery, spent his evenings testing new chemical compounds on himself and his dinner guests in search of a usable anaesthetic. On the night of 4 November 1847, at his home on Queen Street, he and two colleagues inhaled chloroform before supper and were, in one contemporary's words, "under the mahogany in a trice" — out cold on the floor until morning. Within days he'd announced his discovery to the city's medical society, and chloroform swiftly became the anaesthetic of choice for childbirth, later used by Queen Victoria herself.

name: Lister Square
description: Pause in this open square, ringed by glass-fronted offices and apartments, and consider that the man it's named for made spaces like this — anywhere with an operating table — dramatically less likely to kill you. Lister Square sits at the heart of Quartermile, the redevelopment of the old Royal Infirmary site, and honours Joseph Lister, the surgeon whose pioneering antiseptic methods slashed post-operative infection rates and made modern surgery survivable worldwide. The wider development takes its own name from its geography: Quartermile is precisely a quarter of a mile, corner to corner, from Edinburgh Castle and the Royal Mile, a neat bit of measuring that turned a working hospital site into a very literal piece of the city's centre.

name: Lister Housing Co-operative (Georgian Tenements)
description: These weathered Georgian tenements — built between 1816 and 1824 — are buildings that came within a whisker of being bulldozed for a university campus expansion. The turning point came in 1976, when an eight-year-old girl fell on a nearby building site, an accident that galvanised students, lecturers and long-term working-class residents to join forces and fight the demolition. They won, forming a housing co-operative — Scotland's first co-operative registered social landlord — that renovated the tenements between 1978 and 1982. description: Count the corners of the quadrangle and you'll find a turret at each one, but look closer still and notice that no two are quite alike — a deliberate touch of individuality on an otherwise rigidly symmetrical building. These pepper-pot towers, crenellations and castle-like details were meant to impress and even intimidate when the school first rose here from 1628, a statement of wealth from a building fund created by a goldsmith's fortune. Their turreted silhouette has since taken on a life of its own: fans of Harry Potter often point to Heriot's, with its four-house system in Hogwarts-matching colours, as the inspiration for the fictional school — a claim J.K. Rowling herself has denied, insisting Hogwarts was conceived long before she ever saw the building.
interesting_fact_1: Each corner turret is subtly different from the others, a deliberate break from perfect symmetry - and Heriot's four-house system, in colours matching Hogwarts, fuels a popular Harry Potter connection that J.K. Rowling has denied.

name: Ornate Iron Railings
description: Run your eye along the ironwork in front of these tenements and you'll notice the pattern repeats with real precision — swirling finials, evenly spaced verticals, the kind of decorative flourish that Georgian builders added even to something as mundane as a boundary fence. Railings like these once lined nearly every New Town and Georgian street in Edinburgh, but two world wars saw huge numbers melted down for scrap metal, making well-preserved stretches like this one, protected today as part of a listed building, increasingly rare survivors of the city's original streetscape.
interesting_fact_1: Large numbers of Edinburgh's original Georgian railings were removed and melted down for scrap during the world wars.

name: Iron Boot Scraper
description: Crouch down and you'll find it bolted beside the doorway — a simple iron blade, worn smooth at the edge, set there for one very practical purpose. Before Edinburgh's streets were properly paved, this was where residents scraped the mud, horse dung and grime off their boots before stepping inside. It's a small, easily overlooked survivor of an age when getting from the street to your front door was a genuinely messy business, and a reminder that not every piece of the city's history hangs in a museum.
interesting_fact_1: Boot scrapers first turn up in print in the mid-18th century, evolving from hand-wrought to mass-produced cast iron by the 19th century, and Edinburgh's New Town is so thick with them that almost every front door has one - yet most have probably never been used in living memory, since cars replaced horses in the early 20th century and the mud they were built to scrape off simply vanished from the streets.

name: Flower-Decorated Tenement Steps
description: Notice how someone has taken the trouble here — pots crowded onto the stone steps, blooms spilling over the edges, colour against the grey sandstone. It's a small, unofficial act of care, the kind repeated on doorsteps across Edinburgh's tenement streets, where residents quietly claim a few square feet of shared stone as their own. Just a resident deciding that the entrance to their close deserved a bit more life than bare steps alone could offer — a tiny, living rebuttal to the idea that stone stairwells have to stay grey and functional all year round.
interesting_fact_1: There's no plaque or committee behind displays like this — under Scots tenement law the common stair itself must legally be kept clear of obstructions, so these doorstep gardens survive only informally, at the tacit tolerance of neighbours rather than any official sanction.

name: Argyle House - 60s architectural eyesore
description: Crane your neck up at the sheer grey bulk of this precast concrete tower and you'll understand why Edinburgh residents have argued about it for decades — some see a monstrous carbuncle, others a defiant piece of honest modernism worth protecting. Built in 1968 to designs by Michael Laird & Partners, its ten and eleven storeys of raw concrete stand in stark contrast to the sandstone streets around it, earning it a long-running reputation as the city's biggest eyesore. More recently it found unlikely fame as a filming location for Netflix's Dept Q and the TV adaptation of Irvine Welsh's Crime, before its owners announced plans to demolish it entirely for a mixed-use redevelopment, a move architects and heritage campaigners are still fighting to stop.
interesting_fact_1: Despite being widely called Edinburgh's biggest eyesore, some architects have campaigned to save the building from demolition as a distinguished modernist work - and it's found a second life as a filming location, appearing in both Netflix's Dept Q and the TV adaptation of Irvine Welsh's Crime.

name: 6VT Edinburgh City Youth Cafe
description: An unassuming doorway on the Vennel, but step through it and you'll find one of the city centre's few genuinely free social spaces built entirely for young people. 6VT has run as a youth charity here for around two decades, offering a safe drop-in space several nights a week for teenagers and young adults, alongside personal development support, educational workshops and advice services. name: Brown's Place
description: Picture this small, quiet close two centuries ago: the old city wall crumbling nearby, and an enterprising innkeeper spotting an opportunity. James Brown, who ran an inn in the Grassmarket, owned land backing onto the Vennel, which for centuries had marked the very edge of Edinburgh — the city's boundary here stood until 1856. Once the Flodden Wall was demolished as redundant after the Napoleonic Wars, Brown carved a new square out of his back-lands, likely recycling the wall's own stone into his new houses, and the resulting close still bears his name today, tucked beside the surviving Flodden Tower a little further up the Vennel.
interesting_fact_1: Brown's Place was developed by innkeeper James Brown, likely reusing stone salvaged from the demolished Flodden Wall.

name: Stone Basements and Area Wells
description: A sunken stone pit sits behind iron railings at the foot of the building, a small gulf between pavement and wall. These are area wells, a standard feature of Georgian and Victorian tenement design, dug out to let daylight and fresh air reach the basement level below street height, where servants' quarters, sculleries and coal stores were once tucked away out of sight. It's a detail so ordinary it barely registers, yet it quietly reveals how these buildings were once organised — a below-stairs world working just beneath the feet of everyone walking past above.
interesting_fact_1: Live-in servants housed in basements like this could work well over 100 hours a week, summoned by a board of bells at the foot of the stairs - one wired to each room above - while the area well itself doubled as a practical back entrance, letting coal deliveries and tradesmen reach the kitchen door directly without ever using the family's front steps.
